Relative Representations Enable Portable White-Box Monitoring Across Language ModelsThanks: Qualcomm AI Research is an initiative of Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.

Tim Bakker Affiliation: Qualcomm AI Research Email: bakker@qti.qualcomm.com    Christos Louizos Affiliation: Qualcomm AI Research
Abstract

Independently trained autoregressive language models often acquire similar capabilities, but it remains unclear whether their internal representations organize behaviorally relevant information in compatible ways. We show that models do in fact organize information similarly by using specific behavioral probes that operate on compatible representations. This unlocks portable white-box monitoring: a probe developed and validated on one model can be reused when the model changes, without requiring labeled target data. To overcome incompatible native activation coordinates, we express each example through its angular distances to a shared set of anchors. We introduce a global anchored construction that summarizes information from all transformer layers and removes model-specific layer selection, so the same frozen probe can be straightforwardly applied to another model. We evaluate cross-model probe transfer across monitoring tasks on trivia datasets, safety monitoring, and mathematical reasoning. On average, transferred global anchored probes preserve at least 85% of same-model probe AUROC over chance. Anchored probes also support transfer to related datasets, remain robust across model scale and prompt changes, and retain performance better than standard probes after model updates. Transfer is nevertheless task- and target-dependent and can fail even when the monitored property remains strongly decodable in the target model. Overall, global anchoring reveals substantial task-relevant compatibility across independently trained models and provides a practical basis for portable white-box monitoring.

1 Introduction

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis proposes that, as models become more capable, they increasingly converge on a common representational geometry: examples related by the same concepts have similar patterns of similarity and difference across models (Huh et al., 2024). To compare how models organize examples, Moschella et al. (2023) introduce relative representations introduce relative representations and show that they preserve input data information across encoder models. We ask whether relative representations also preserve information about model behavior: do independently trained autoregressive language models represent the results of their own computations in functionally compatible ways?

We test this question by asking whether a probe trained to predict a behavioral property in one model remains predictive in another. Native activations cannot support this test directly: models can differ in width and depth, and even equal-width residual streams can use different bases. We therefore use relative representations: each activation is represented by its angular distances to a shared anchor set, yielding one coordinate per anchor with the same anchor identities across models.

The simplest anchored construction measures each example’s distances to the anchors at one chosen layer and trains a local anchored probe on the resulting representation. Such a probe still requires compatible layer choices across models, and the useful depth can vary by task and model. We instead introduce global anchored representations, which concatenate residual-stream activations from all transformer layers at the monitored position before computing angular distances to the shared anchor set. Because each model’s anchor activations are computed once and cached, each monitored example can be compared with all anchors in one batched operation. The resulting representation has one coordinate per anchor, so a source-trained probe can consume it across models even when their widths and depths differ. Global aggregation is not required for probe transfer, but it removes cross-model layer selection and provides a depth-free default for comparing representations.

Successful cross-model probe transfer has a direct practical implication for white-box monitoring or probing, which uses internal activations to predict properties of model behavior. Prior work has used such signals to anticipate answer quality (Gottesman and Geva, 2024; Snyder et al., 2024), detect hallucinations (Orgad et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024), and monitor safety-relevant behavior (McKenzie et al., 2025). Activation probes are also actively deployed as misuse mitigations in user-facing models (Kramár et al., 2026). These monitors are typically developed for a single model because their decision rules are expressed in that model’s activation coordinates. A new model may therefore require collecting labeled activations, selecting a layer, and fitting and validating another probe; model or deployment changes can also degrade an existing monitor (Kramár et al., 2026; Duan, 2026). Cross-model probe transfer would instead let a validated monitor be reused without target-model labels or a learned target-specific adapter. This amortizes probe development costs and, for instance, allows practitioners to develop probes when access to models and data may be restricted.

We evaluate anchored probes on trivia datasets, safety monitoring, and mathematical reasoning. Our main findings are:

  • •

    When trained and evaluated on the same model, global anchored probes perform comparably to standard probes. Transferred global anchored probes preserve at least 85% of the same-model anchored-probe AUROC performance over chance. This provides evidence that models indeed share task-relevant relational structure at the level of their internal computations.

  • •

    The same approach supports joint transfer to a new model and a related dataset without using labeled examples from the new deployment setting. This allows a monitor developed with accessible models and data to be reused when both the deployed model and its data distribution change.

  • •

    We test portability across model scale, model updates, prompt variants, and external model families. Transfer can remain strong across large scale and prompt changes, and anchored probes are more robust to model updates than standard probes. Transfer is weak for some models with poor task performance and is task-dependent across external model families. We additionally provide evidence that transfer tolerates non-identical textual anchors and noisy anchor mappings.

2 Related Work

Our central question is whether independently trained language models organize information about their own behavior in compatible ways. We test this by freezing a behavioral probe trained on one model and evaluating it on another in shared anchor-relative coordinates. This connects work on representational convergence with behavioral probing;

Representational convergence and relative representations.

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis proposes that increasingly capable models converge in the relationships they encode among examples (Huh et al., 2024). Moschella et al. (2023) provide the closest methodological precursor: their relative representations encode examples by similarity to fixed anchors, enabling zero-shot communication and transfer of classification or reconstruction components across seeds and architectures. We ask whether this relational compatibility extends to information about a model’s own behavior. Indra representations (Lu et al., 2025) use angular-distance profiles to improve robustness of downstream classifiers and cross-modal retrieval. They do not consider cross-model probe transfer and use full distance profiles over a dataset rather than a fixed set of common anchors. Model stitching (Bansal et al., 2021) tests functional compatibility by connecting the lower layers of one model to the upper layers of another through a trained low-capacity adapter. Unlike our approach, it learns a bridge between the two representation spaces.

Probing behavioral information.

Probes have found decodable syntactic, semantic, spatial, temporal, and behavioral information in model representations (Conneau et al., 2018; Tenney et al., 2019; Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024; Zou et al., 2023). Internal-state monitors use such signals to anticipate answer quality or characterize model knowledge (Ferrando et al., 2024; Gottesman and Geva, 2024; Joshi et al., 2024; Afzal et al., 2025), detect hallucinations (CH-Wang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Orgad et al., 2024; Simhi et al., 2024; Snyder et al., 2024), and identify safety-relevant behavior (McKenzie et al., 2025; Kramár et al., 2026). These studies establish that a model’s activations contain information about its own behavior. Cross-model probe transfer tests whether that information is organized compatibly across models. The interpretation of probe performance also depends on distribution, probe capacity, and layer choice (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Voita and Titov, 2020; Belinkov, 2022; Levinstein and Herrmann, 2023; Mallen et al., 2023; Kramár et al., 2026; Min et al., 2026). Cross-layer architectures aggregate information from several layers within one model (Suresh et al., 2025; Nordby et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026), while Liang and Wang (2025) use Bayesian optimization to select a single probe insertion layer. Our global construction uses the whole depth of a model to produce anchor-indexed coordinates, so we can test compatibility without choosing corresponding layers across architectures.

Cross-model monitoring as an application.

ACT-ViT is the closest prior system for cross-model white-box monitoring (Bar-Shalom et al., 2025). It pools activation tensors, maps each language model through its own linear adapter, and applies a shared vision-transformer backbone pretrained on labeled activations from multiple model–dataset pairs. Learned source–target mappers similarly transfer activation-space interventions by fitting a model-pair-specific bridge (Oozeer et al., 2025). Both approaches learn a new mapping for each target: ACT-ViT trains a new adapter for every language model, while intervention transfer trains a bridge for every source–target pair. We instead express each model relative to the same shared examples, so transferring a monitoring probe to a new target requires only an unlabeled pass over the anchor set and no learned target-specific component.

3 Methodology

Our method expresses each model’s activations through their relations to shared anchors, creating common coordinates in which a probe trained on one model can be applied to another. This transfer supports portable monitoring and tests predictive compatibility across models.

3.1 Anchored Representations

Let hℓ(m)​(x)h_{\ell}^{(m)}(x) denote the residual-stream activation of model mm at layer ℓ\ell for example xx. Let AD={a1,…,ak}A_{D}=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{k}\} be a set of kk anchor examples drawn from the training split of dataset DD. Every model processes the same indexed anchor set. Unless stated otherwise, anchor activations are taken at the final prompt position, immediately before generation. In an appendix sensitivity analysis, we instead average activations over each anchor’s generated completion (Appendix C.5). Following the relative representation of Moschella et al. (2023), a local anchored representation at layer ℓ\ell is

rℓ(m)​(x,AD)=[s⁡(hℓ(m)​(x),hℓ(m)​(a1)),…,s⁡(hℓ(m)​(x),hℓ(m)​(ak))],r_{\ell}^{(m)}(x;A_{D})=\big[s(h_{\ell}^{(m)}(x),h_{\ell}^{(m)}(a_{1})),\dots,s(h_{\ell}^{(m)}(x),h_{\ell}^{(m)}(a_{k}))\big],

where s⁡(⋅,⋅)s(\cdot,\cdot) is a relational distance function. The representation has one coordinate for each anchor identity. Its dimension is determined by the number of anchors and is independent of the model’s hidden size.

A probe can be trained on rℓ(m)​(x,AD)r_{\ell}^{(m)}(x;A_{D}) using the same supervision as a probe on the native activation hℓ(m)​(x)h_{\ell}^{(m)}(x). We call the former an anchored probe. A standard probe uses the native activation and serves as the same-model baseline.

3.2 Global Anchored Representations

The direct local construction still requires a choice of probing layer. Our main method instead summarizes the residual stream across the complete network. For model mm with LmL_{m} transformer layers, define

g(m)​(x)=concat⁡(h0(m)​(x),…,hLm−1(m)​(x)).g^{(m)}(x)=\operatorname{concat}\big(h_{0}^{(m)}(x),\dots,h_{L_{m}-1}^{(m)}(x)\big).

We then compute the global anchored representation

R(m)​(x,AD)=[s⁡(g(m)​(x),g(m)​(a1)),…,s⁡(g(m)​(x),g(m)​(ak))].R^{(m)}(x;A_{D})=\big[s(g^{(m)}(x),g^{(m)}(a_{1})),\dots,s(g^{(m)}(x),g^{(m)}(a_{k}))\big].

The intermediate vector g(m)​(x)g^{(m)}(x) can have a different dimension for every model, but R(m)​(x,AD)R^{(m)}(x;A_{D}) always has dimension kk and the same anchor indexing. A probe trained on one model can therefore be applied to another model’s representation even when the models differ in width and depth. In contrast to a local anchored probe, the global construction also removes the need to choose corresponding layers. Figure 3 in the Appendix illustrates our construction.

Following the angular construction used for Indra representations (Lu et al., 2025), we use

s⁡(u,v)=arccos⁡(u⋅v∥u∥​∥v∥).s(u,v)=\arccos\!\left(\frac{u\cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert\,\lVert v\rVert}\right).

This is the angular distance in radians. For global representations it is computed between whole-network vectors; for local representations it is computed between activations from one layer.

3.3 Task Settings

We evaluate the probes in three data settings: Trivia settings test whether probes retain information about model behavior and answer correctness, Guard Distillation tests probe performance for safety monitoring, and Online MATH tests whether probes can predict correctness of reasoning models on math questions. Safety monitoring is a common production use-case for probes (Kramár et al., 2026), and probes for early-correctness prediction during reasoning have been used for both efficiency (Zhang et al., 2025) and test time scaling (Ni et al., 2026).

Trivia.

We use TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022), SciQ (Welbl et al., 2017), and MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a) in binary-choice and four-choice formats. Each prompt asks the model to produce an answer option. We read the residual stream at the final prompt position, immediately before answer generation. Output Prediction predicts the option selected by the model, while ground-truth (GT) Prediction predicts the correct option. Prior work shows that pre-answer activations carry information about answer quality and knowledge state (Snyder et al., 2024; Gottesman and Geva, 2024). TruthfulQA, SciQ, and MMLU contain 817, 1,000, and 783 examples, respectively. We split each dataset 60/20/20 for training, validation, and testing, and sample 300 anchors from its training split.

Guard Distillation.

We use prompts from BeaverTails (Ji et al., 2023) and Toxic-chat (Lin et al., 2023). Each monitored model generates completions, and Llama-Guard-3-8B (Llama Team, 2024) labels the resulting prompt–completion pair as safe or unsafe. The probe predicts this binary label from the monitored model’s completion-token activations. Standard probes average residual-stream activations over completion tokens at each layer. For anchored probes, we instead compute an anchor-relative representation for each completion token and then average those representations. For each dataset, we use 1,000 prompts split 60/20/20 for training, validation, and testing. The 600 training prompts serve as anchors.

Online MATH.

We additionally train probes to predict whether a generated solution to a MATH problem will ultimately be correct (Hendrycks et al., 2021b). At checkpoints during generation, we average each layer’s residual-stream activations over all tokens generated so far. Our primary comparisons use 2,000 training examples and the 128-token checkpoint, selected before probe fitting because 92.8–99.6% of source training and validation trajectories had not yet ended at that point. We use a separate 500-example validation set and 300 anchors sampled from the training data, and evaluate on MATH-500. Appendix D.1 reports results with 1,000 training examples and at the 64- and 256-token checkpoints.

Across all three settings, we also evaluate transfer to related datasets: among the trivia datasets, between BeaverTails and Toxic-chat, and from MATH to GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021). We test both dataset transfer within one model and joint transfer to a new dataset and model. Labels from the target dataset are used only for final scoring.

3.4 Cross-Model Transfer and Evaluation Protocol

Let msm_{s} be a source model and mtm_{t} a target model. We fit a probe on R(ms)​(x,AD)R^{(m_{s})}(x;A_{D}), freeze it, and apply it to R(mt)​(x,AD)R^{(m_{t})}(x;A_{D}). Successful transfer means that this frozen probe remains predictive on the target model’s anchored representations. Deployment on the target requires one unlabeled setup pass over the anchor set, in addition to the usual forward pass for each monitored example; crucially, we do not require target-model labels, a learned target adapter, or probe retraining.

The trivia and Guard Distillation evaluations share a six-model pool: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Llama Team, 2024), Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Qwen Team, 2025), which we refer to as Qwen3-4B-Instruct below. Before extracting activations, we screened candidate models on MATH. Several models in the trivia and Guard Distillation pool produced too few correct solutions for reliable probe training and evaluation, so we use a separate four-model pool for online mathematical correctness: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-12B-Instruct (Team, 2025b; Team, 2025a).

Within each pool, every model serves in turn as a target, with the other models available as sources. For each target, Transfer directly applies every non-target source probe and averages the resulting AUROCs. When several source probes are available, their transfer reliability can be estimated before deployment by testing each one on the other labeled models in the source pool. Our source-only calibration procedure (reported as Transfer (cal)) selects the source probe with the highest mean validation AUROC on those other source-pool models and then applies it to the held-out target. No target labels enter calibration. Calibration uses all available source models within the corresponding pool and is intended to improve deployment performance. For local anchored probes, source and target activations are taken at the same relative depth dd across the two models. We apply the direct and calibrated procedures separately at each depth.

We distinguish two evaluation regimes. An in-pool target is one member of a prespecified model pool held out in turn while the remaining models provide source probes and calibration data. An external target belongs to a model family outside the corresponding source and calibration pool. For external targets, source selection is completed entirely within that pool before the selected probe is scored on the new model. Dataset construction, model settings, and optimization details appear in Appendix A.

4 Experiments

We use behavioral monitoring tasks as a functional test of whether independently trained models organize behaviorally relevant information in compatible ways. If anchor-relative coordinates preserve a behavioral signal within each model and a probe’s fixed decision rule remains predictive across models, then the models share task-relevant relational structure in a form usable by the same monitor. We first test these two conditions, then ask when this compatibility persists across external model families, related data distributions, layer choices, model scale, model updates, and prompt formats. Supporting analyses examine low-FPR recall and the relational geometry of the anchors.

We use a linear probe on native activations at prespecified relative depth 0.80.8 as the standard baseline; the basis for this choice is reported in Appendix Figures 7 and 11. We report area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for all three settings. We additionally report recall at 10% FPR in Appendices B.4, C.2, and D.2. Full implementation details appear in Appendix A. We examine anchor-count variants, attention probes, and other nonlinear probes in Appendices B.8, C.9, and C.11.

4.1 Same-Model Decodability

Anchoring replaces each model’s native residual coordinates with a common, anchor-indexed representation, so we first test whether that change sacrifices predictive information, before testing portability. Standard and Anchored probes receive the same labels and differ only in their input representation. The anchored representations are also substantially more compact: every model has 300 coordinates for trivia and MATH or 600 for Guard Distillation, compared with native residual widths from 2,048 dimensions for Qwen2.5-3B to 4,096 for Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B.

Trivia Output Prediction is near ceiling within each model: Standard and Anchored probes both reach 99.5–100.0 AUROC across the six dataset variants (Appendix B.2). For the more discriminating GT Prediction setting, Anchored probes outperform Standard probes on four variants and trail them on two; the largest difference in either direction is 1.4 AUROC points (Table 1). Guard Distillation also has small same-model gaps: Standard and Anchored score 96.5 and 94.9 on BeaverTails, and 88.6 and 87.5 on Toxic-chat (Table 2). For MATH, the global Anchored probe reaches 81.8 AUROC, compared with 77.9 for the Standard probe (Table 3). Anchoring therefore preserves nearly all of the tested same-model linear predictive signal in trivia and safety, while improving same-model decodability in MATH.

4.2 Cross-Model Probe Transfer

We now test the central question: after fitting a probe on one source model, does its decision rule remain predictive when applied unchanged to another model? We test this across trivia and Guard Distillation in the six-model pool, and across online MATH in its separate four-model pool. Calibration uses all available non-target source models: five for trivia and Guard Distillation, and three for online MATH. Appendices B.2 and C.1 additionally report how trivia and Guard Distillation transfer changes as the available source pool grows from one to five models; Appendix D.1 reports the corresponding one-to-three-source progression for online MATH.

Averaged separately within each setting, calibrated global transfer preserves 99.1% of same-model Anchored AUROC above chance for trivia Output Prediction, 90.7% for trivia GT Prediction, 85.0% for Guard Distillation, and 88.1% for online MATH. Tables  1, 2, and 3 report the corresponding results. Trivia Output Prediction also remains near ceiling after transfer: calibrated AUROC ranges from 98.3 to 99.9 (Appendix B.2). This result shows that features of a model’s selected answer are strongly transferable, so the main trivia table focuses on the more discriminating GT Prediction task.

Calibrated transfer remains predictive in all three settings, although the loss relative to same-model Anchored probes varies. For trivia Output Prediction, calibrated transfer is at most 1.5 AUROC points below the same-model Anchored probe across all six variants; GT Prediction is within 0.6 points on MMLU and SciQ. For online MATH, a probe trained on one model’s solution prefixes predicts whether another model’s solution will ultimately be correct: global calibrated transfer reaches 78.0 AUROC, 3.8 points below global same-model Anchored performance. Notably, this matches the 77.9 AUROC of Standard probes trained directly on each target. Guard Distillation shows substantial but less complete transfer, reaching 86.4 on BeaverTails and 83.6 on Toxic-chat, compared with same-model Anchored AUROCs of 94.9 and 87.5. The common anchor coordinates therefore support reuse of a fixed behavioral decision rule across all three settings, with transfer losses relative to same-model probes that vary by task. This functional transfer provides evidence that anchored representations organize task-relevant information compatibly across models. To show that matching dimensions do not explain transfer, we transfer standard probes between Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, which have the same residual width and depth. These probes perform at chance level, while anchored probes transfer strongly (Appendices B.10 and C.12).

Binary TruthfulQA GT Prediction is the main exception to the strong trivia results: calibrated transfer reaches 73.1 AUROC, compared with 89.1 same-model. The gap is concentrated in Llama-3.2-3B, the least accurate TruthfulQA target; its same-model probe remains strong, but all incoming probes perform near chance (Figure 2). Across the 36 trivia target–dataset cells, target answer accuracy is strongly associated with incoming GT Prediction transfer. Transfer may therefore be less reliable for low-accuracy targets, although the strong same-model probe shows that there remains decodable target signal (Appendix B.9). Recall at 10% FPR reveals larger transfer losses, particularly for binary TruthfulQA GT Prediction and Guard Distillation (Appendices B.4, C.2, and D.2).

4.3 When Does Predictive Compatibility Persist?

We next test whether this compatibility extends beyond the original model pools and persists under related data and other deployment changes.

4.3.1 External Model Families

The preceding experiments hold out each target from a prespecified model pool. To test whether portability extends beyond those development pools, we keep each pool fixed and evaluate additional models. The transferred probes and their source choices are fixed before external target models and labels are introduced. For trivia and Guard Distillation, the new targets are OLMo-3-7B (Team, 2025b), Gemma-3-12B (Team, 2025a), and GPT-OSS-20B (OpenAI, 2025). For MATH, GPT-OSS is held out. Table 4 summarizes these results.

Trivia GT Prediction reaches 90.2–94.4 AUROC across the three external families, matching or exceeding the 89.6 average for held-out targets in the original pool. Output Prediction remains near saturation at 98.6–99.6 AUROC (Table 4). Guard Distillation is more heterogeneous, with Toxic-chat transfer ranging from 66.9 to 87.6. BeaverTails estimates are high-variance because only 1.0–4.8% of completions are unsafe for these newer models. Appendices B.5 and C.3 report the full results.

For MATH, transfer to GPT-OSS remains near chance at 52.4–53.1 AUROC across the two source-training sizes. Appendix D.3 reports target-trained probes, which reach 78.5–78.7 AUROC and show that correctness remains linearly decodable in GPT-OSS. The decision boundary learned from the source models is therefore not predictive for GPT-OSS. GPT-OSS is also the only mixture-of-experts model in our external MATH evaluation. Its expert routing may contribute to the failure, although the current comparison cannot separate that possibility from other architectural and training differences. The failure is task-specific: trivia probes transfer strongly to GPT-OSS and the other external targets. External-family transfer therefore varies by model–task pair, but remains strong for several targets outside the calibration pool.

4.3.2 Related Data Distributions

The practical value of compatible representations is greatest when both the deployed model and its data change, since collecting and validating target labels may be prohibitive. Activation probes can degrade under distribution shifts even when the model is fixed (Orgad et al., 2024; Levinstein and Herrmann, 2023; Kramár et al., 2026; Min et al., 2026). We therefore use same-model standard probes as a reference and ask whether anchoring preserves or improves related-data robustness while also enabling a simultaneous model change. A joint shift approximates, for instance, a restricted-access setting in which a monitor developed on an accessible model and dataset is applied locally to a different model on related private data without sharing the target model or data. We evaluate three such data shifts: among trivia datasets, between BeaverTails and Toxic-chat, and from MATH to GSM8K. The anchors and labels used to fit or calibrate probes always come from the source dataset; target labels are used only for final scoring.

When the model is fixed, global anchored probes outperform standard probes in every trivia GT Prediction direction, averaging 87.0 AUROC with gains of up to 13.1 points, and on MATH-to-GSM8K, at 75.3 versus 63.0. They roughly match standard probes on average for Guard Distillation, at 77.9 versus 78.3. When both the model and dataset change, trivia transfer averages 83.1 directly and 86.1 after source calibration; calibrated Guard transfer reaches 65.1 from BeaverTails to Toxic-chat and 79.6 in the reverse direction; and calibrated MATH-to-GSM8K transfer reaches 70.5. Despite the simultaneous model change, MATH-to-GSM8K transfer remains 7.4 points above a standard probe applied within the same model.

Guard probe transfer shows that performance across related data is not uniformly reliable. To examine this gap, we compare each target example’s distance to its nearest source anchor (Appendix C.6). Target examples are farther from the source anchors when moving from curated BeaverTails prompts to real-world Toxic-chat conversations, suggesting that transfer quality is related to how well the source anchors cover the target data. Full results appear in Appendices B.6, C.4, and D.4.

4.3.3 Other Robustness Checks

Layer selection.

The global construction avoids choosing layers across models. We compare it with local probes whose depths are selected using source-model validation data. Across all three task families, local probes do not consistently outperform global probes, making the global construction a robust depth-free default (Appendices B.3, C.7, D.1).

Model scale.

We test transfer across a same-family Llama 3.x scale gap on MMLU. Transfer from the 1B model to the 70B model reaches 94.8 AUROC, close to the 96.0 AUROC of a probe trained directly on the 70B model. This suggests that labeled probe development may be done on the much less expensive 1B model, and deployed on the 70B model at little performance loss. Transfer into the 1B target — the reverse direction — is near chance, and the 1B same-model probe reaches only 68.2 AUROC, reinforcing the earlier pattern that transfer into weak targets is difficult (Appendix B.9).

Model updates.

A deployed monitor can become outdated when its model is fine-tuned after probe training. Following the setup of Duan (2026), we train global anchored safety probes on XSTest safety data (Röttger et al., 2024) for Qwen2.5-3B and 7B. We then fix the probes, fine-tune the Qwen models on refusal data with LoRA and QLoRA, and evaluate probe robustness under this distribution shift. We find that global anchored probes are more robust to both model quantization and updates than standard probes and local anchored probes (Appendix E).

Prompt format.

We compare the standard trivia prompt with minimal and verbose variants while holding the tasks, examples, and models fixed. Under the minimal prompt, calibrated transfer changes by only about one AUROC point while same-model probes degrade more, suggesting that transferred probes are less sensitive to this tested change (Appendix B.7).

Anchor content and correspondence.

Finally, we ask whether anchors must exactly match across models. In Guard Distillation, same-dataset Transfer (cal) changes by at most 2.7 AUROC points when each anchor is represented by averaging over that model’s generated completion rather than at the final token of the shared prompt, even though the completion — and thus the anchor — differs between models (Appendix C.5). In a separate test, we hide the anchor identities and recover 20.7% of their cross-model matches using only pairwise distances, compared with 0.16% by chance (Appendix C.10). Probes applied to the partially recovered space retain more than 90%90\% of the original AUROC. Together, these results suggest that transfer can tolerate non-identical textual anchors and substantial noise in the anchor mapping, consistent with reliance on the anchor set’s broader semantic organization rather than exact one-to-one correspondence.

5 Conclusion

We show that relative representations can support functional reuse of model representations for white-box monitoring of independently trained autoregressive language models. Across trivia, safety monitoring, and mathematical reasoning, anchored coordinates retain useful same-model signal, and probes trained on one model remain predictive on others. Transfer of a fixed behavioral probe provides substantial evidence that the models share task-relevant relational organization.

This representation provides a practical route to portable white-box monitoring. Anchored probes support joint changes of model and related data, large same-family scale changes, and prompt variations. They also retain more performance than standard probes after model updates. Reusing a validated probe can therefore reduce repeated labeling, tuning, and validation as models and deployment conditions change, while our global construction avoids model-specific layer selection.

We note that portability remains conditional: transfer weakens for some weakly-performing target models and can occasionally fail even when the monitored property remains decodable in the target model. Future work may develop principled anchor selection, develop methods for predicting transfer failures — potentially based on anchor-similarity or coverage measures — and extend the approach to long-context, multi-turn, and multimodal settings. Overall, our results show that independently trained autoregressive language models share substantial relevant relational organization in their learned features and demonstrate a practical method for reusing white-box monitors across models.

Appendix Contents

Appendix A Implementation details

We compare standard probes, trained directly on residual-stream activations, with anchored probes, trained on anchor-relative representations of the same activations. We use two anchored representations. In the global setting, we build a single whole-network representation by concatenating the relevant residual-stream vectors from all transformer layers and then mapping that vector into anchor-relative coordinates. The layer vectors are concatenated raw, with no per-layer normalization before computing angular distance. In the local setting, we build a separate anchor-relative representation for each transformer layer, parameterized by a relative depth d∈[0,1]d\in[0,1]. The global representation removes the need to choose a probing layer and yields a fixed probe dimensionality determined only by the number of anchors, enabling cross-model transfer even when models differ in hidden size and depth.

Our global anchored results are compared against the standard single-layer absolute-probe baseline evaluated at relative depth 0.80.8. For local anchored probes, we evaluate at matched source and target relative depth dd: the source probe and target representation are taken at the same depth, and the Transfer and Transfer (cal) procedures are applied independently at each dd used in the depth sweep. The resulting validation-based depth comparisons are reported in Appendices B.3, C.7, and D.1; GuardQA’s corresponding analysis appears in Appendix F.4. Unless stated otherwise, all reported results average over three seeds.

A.1 Shared protocol

The following conventions apply to the Trivia, Guard Distillation, online MATH, and GuardQA protocols unless a setting-specific subsection states otherwise. GuardQA is an auxiliary safety setting that asks the monitored model to classify a stored prompt–completion pair as safe or unsafe in an A/B question; its full motivation and protocol appear in Appendix A.7.

Layer and token-position convention.

Stored layer activations correspond to transformer-block outputs. We index these layers from 00 to Lm−1L_{m}-1 for a model with LmL_{m} transformer blocks; the token-embedding layer and unembedding/output head are not included. For the single-token Trivia and GuardQA experiments, probes read the final prompt position: after the model has processed the full prompt, but before the first answer token has been generated. Guard Distillation instead probes monitored completion-token representations. Its main linear experiment uses single-token anchors taken at the final prompt position.

Relative-depth mapping.

For local probes, relative depth is computed as d⁡(ℓ,Lm)=ℓ/(Lm−1)d(\ell;L_{m})=\ell/(L_{m}-1) for zero-indexed transformer-block layer ℓ\ell. When mapping layers across models with different depths, the first and last transformer-block layers are pinned to the first and last bins, respectively. Intermediate layers are assigned to the nearest relative-depth bin center, using rounding. This convention lets local transfer compare source and target layers at matched relative depth while excluding embeddings and unembedding from the layer count.

Anchors, distance function, and scaling.

Anchors are randomly sampled from the training split using the seed for the run. They may overlap with examples used to train the probe, but they are not sampled from validation or test examples. For a fixed dataset, seed, and anchor configuration, the same anchor IDs and order are used for every model, so the anchored coordinates are indexed by the same datapoints across models. Related-data transfer retains the source dataset’s anchor set, as described in Appendix A.6. Our main distance function is angular distance, the arccos\arccos of cosine similarity. In global mode, raw per-layer vectors are concatenated first and the angular distance is computed on the resulting whole-network vector; no per-layer normalization is applied before concatenation. Unless otherwise noted, probe feature normalization uses the source probe’s stored training-set mean and standard deviation (or scaler). In cross-model applications, we do not refit normalization statistics on the target model’s validation or test activations.

Metrics.

We evaluate probe performance using two complementary metrics. AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) summarizes discrimination quality over all possible thresholds and is insensitive to class imbalance; it is our primary metric in the main text. R@0.1FPR reports the true-positive rate at a fixed false-positive budget and is more informative for deployment scenarios in which the cost of false positives is high (e.g., safety monitoring with a low-tolerance alert threshold). Both metrics are standard in the internal-monitoring literature (Snyder et al., 2024; Obeso et al., 2025). We compute AUROC with scikit-learn’s roc_auc_score. Binary cells use the usual binary AUROC; multiclass cells use one-vs-rest macro averaging. The four-choice Trivia settings have no substantial class imbalance, so this averaging choice does not drive the reported trends. We report AUROC for all cells (binary and multiclass) and R@0.1FPR for the binary trivia variants, both GuardQA datasets, Guard Distillation, and online MATH.

For R@0.1FPR, the positive class is task-specific. For binary answer-choice settings (binary Trivia and GuardQA Output Prediction/GT Prediction), recall is computed for the encoded class 1 answer, i.e., answer B in the A/B format; since answer positions are randomized and close to balanced, this is only a reporting convention. For Guard Distillation, recall is instead unsafe-positive: true positives are unsafe completions detected by the probe, and false positives are safe completions incorrectly flagged as unsafe. For online MATH, the positive class is a correct solution. A few transferred MATH and GSM8K predictions have tied scores at the operating boundary, so we report deterministic expected recall under randomized tie-breaking at exactly 10% FPR.

Dataset and answer-position balance.

Tables 6 and 7 summarize the label-position and model-output distributions used by the Trivia and GuardQA experiments. The tables average over the six-model pool and three seeds. Binary Trivia and GuardQA ground-truth positions are close to balanced across A/B; the four-choice Trivia variants are similarly balanced across A/B/C/D. GuardQA A/B positions are randomized independently of the raw safe/unsafe label, so the probe target for safety prediction is balanced even though the underlying Guard safe/unsafe labels are not. Guard Distillation uses the raw Llama Guard safety labels directly; its realized label balance is reported in Appendix A.3.

Cross-model calibration averaging.

Section 3.4 defines direct transfer and our source-only calibration procedure. Global representations leave only a choice of source probe: each model yields one anchor-indexed vector per example, so there is no source-layer or target-layer search. We use a leave-one-target-out procedure in both the six-model Trivia, Guard Distillation, and GuardQA pools and the four-model online-MATH pool.

For the six-model pools, every target contributes exactly once per table cell:

  • •

    Transfer (naive transfer): for each of the 6 models as target, average the test AUROC of the 5 remaining source probes applied to that target. Then average over the 6 targets. The reported number is therefore a mean over the 6×5=306\times 5=30 off-diagonal source-target pairs in the confusion matrix (Figure 2 shows one such matrix).

  • •

    Transfer (cal-NN): for each target, enumerate all size-NN source subsets that exclude that target (combinations). Within each subset, score each candidate source probe by its mean validation AUROC on the other models in the subset, select the best source, and record its test AUROC on the in-pool target. Average over subsets, then over targets. This source-selection step uses only source-model validation labels.

The N=1N=1 case is equivalent to naive Transfer, since a singleton source subset contains no source-selection decision; the six-model tables therefore show Transfer followed by calibrated columns for larger source subsets.

Online MATH uses the same leave-one-target-out logic with three candidate sources per target: direct transfer averages the three source probes, giving 4×3=124\times 3=12 directed source–target pairs. For calibrated transfer, we score each candidate source probe on the other two source models by its mean validation AUROC across the 64-, 128-, and 256-token checkpoints, then apply the selected source model’s checkpoint-specific probes unchanged to the held-out target. We do not report a calibration-pool progression for MATH because each target has only three available sources.

Calibration assumes labeled validation data for the available source models, but no labels, adapters, or retraining for the in-pool target model. The standard error reported alongside each mean reflects variability across the three random seeds (affecting data splits, anchor selection, and probe training): SE=s/n\text{SE}=s/\sqrt{n}, with ss the sample standard deviation using Bessel’s correction and n=3n=3. It does not attempt to summarize heterogeneity across models or directed source–target pairs.

A.2 Trivia setting

Our trivia experiments use TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022), SciQ (Welbl et al., 2017), and MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a) in both binary-choice and four-choice variants. We load TruthfulQA from domenicrosati/TruthfulQA and SciQ from allenai/sciq, in both cases drawing examples from the train split of the dataset. For MMLU we use the miscellaneous subject configuration of cais/mmlu, because its general-knowledge questions are closest in style to the trivia setting, and we draw examples from MMLU’s test split, which is the canonical evaluation split for that benchmark. These source splits are used as example pools; each pool is then internally split into 60% train, 20% validation, and 20% test for probe training and evaluation. We probe the residual stream at the final prompt position, immediately before the model emits its selected option, which is the point most directly tied to answer selection. For global anchored probes, we extract this token position from every transformer-block layer, concatenate the resulting raw layer vectors, and then build the anchor-relative representation from that concatenated vector.

The default trivia prompt uses a system instruction telling the model to answer the multiple-choice question with only the letter corresponding to its choice. The user message then contains the question, the answer options labeled A, B, …, and a final Answer: cue. In other words, the default prompt has the form

[System] You are a helpful assistant. Answer the multiple choice question by responding with only the letter A/B/…
[User] {question}
A. {answer A}
B. {answer B}
…
Answer:

Multiple-choice options are constructed per sample with deterministic randomization. For TruthfulQA we sample one correct answer from the available reference-correct set, then sample the required number of incorrect answers without replacement; for SciQ and MMLU we sample distractors analogously. After assembling the answer set, we draw a random insertion position for the correct answer, so the correct label is randomized across A/B (or A/B/C/D) rather than fixed to a particular letter. To make this reproducible, each sample uses a fixed per-sample seed (generation seed + sample index), so answer sampling and label placement are stable across runs. If a sample has fewer incorrect options than requested (mainly relevant for multiclass TruthfulQA), we keep the sample and use all available incorrect answers rather than dropping it.

A.3 Guard Distillation setting

Guard Distillation evaluates anchored probes on binary safety-monitoring labels for monitored prompt-completion pairs. It uses the six models in Table 5 and prompts from BeaverTails and Toxic-chat. For each monitored model, we generate a completion, label the resulting prompt-completion pair with Llama-Guard-3-8B (Llama Team, 2024), and train probes on the monitored completion-token representations to predict the binary Guard Distillation label. The resulting probes act as distilled Guard models: white-box safety monitors that approximate Guard labels from internal activations. Because anchored representations are shared across models, the Guard Distillation experiment tests whether such monitors can transfer across model families.

The Guard Distillation runs use a fixed 1,000 prompts per dataset. A separate Qwen3-4B screening pass generates and Llama-Guard-labels a completion for every available prompt. From these labels, we use seeded stratified sampling to target 40% unsafe examples within each 60/20/20 split, capped by the number of unsafe screening examples available. Sampling within each Guard label also preserves the relative proportions of the source dataset’s safety labels. The screening completions are used only to choose prompt IDs and are not reused in the monitoring experiment. We then generate model-specific completions for those prompts with temperature 0.30.3, top-p=0.95p=0.95, and at most 800800 new tokens, re-label each model-specific prompt-completion pair with Llama-Guard, and use the selected train, validation, and test IDs. We supply each dataset prompt as a user message under the model’s native chat template and do not add a task-specific system message. For standard probes, we average raw residual-stream activations over the monitored completion tokens at each layer; the all-layer standard control then concatenates these layerwise means. For anchored probes, we first compute the angular-distance feature vector separately for each completion token and then average those feature vectors. The linear probe uses 600600 anchors and C=0.1C=0.1.

We score each prompt–completion pair by formatting the prompt as a user message and the completion as an assistant message with Llama Guard’s native chat template. Llama-Guard-3-8B decodes greedily for at most 10 tokens. We read the safe and unsafe probabilities from the logits at its first generated safety-label token and assign whichever label has higher probability.

The main Guard Distillation linear AUROC, recall, and model-family results use single-token anchors. We take each anchor activation at the final prompt position, immediately before the model emits its first completion token, as in Trivia and GuardQA. Appendix C also reports ablations with mean-token anchors. These variants instead average each anchor prompt’s completion-token activations before computing angular distance per token to obtain the final anchored representation.

Table 9 reports the realized Llama Guard label balance for each monitored model’s Guard Distillation completions. Unsafe completions are rare for most model–dataset pairs, making probe training class-imbalanced. Mistral is an exception on BeaverTails: its mean unsafe rate is substantially higher than those of the other monitored models. On the external targets, BeaverTails has especially few unsafe completions: the mean unsafe rates are 1.0% for OLMo-3, 1.5% for GPT-OSS, and 4.8% for Gemma-3. One OLMo-3 seed contains no unsafe BeaverTails test completion, so its AUROC is undefined and excluded from the AUROC mean; the corresponding prevalence summary still uses all three seeds. Toxic-chat unsafe rates range from 9.0% to 11.8%, and all Toxic-chat seed-level AUROCs are defined.

A.4 Online MATH correctness setting

The online correctness experiment generates solutions to MATH problems (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) and predicts, from an intermediate prefix, whether the completed solution will be correct. The in-pool model set is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-12B-Instruct. Each problem is supplied as a user message that asks the model to show its reasoning and place its final expression in \boxed{...}. We use each model’s native chat template and do not add a task-specific system message. Each example’s layer feature is the mean residual-stream activation over the generated tokens available at checkpoints 64, 128, and 256. The Standard baseline and fixed local comparison use relative depth 0.80.8; global features concatenate the prefix means from every layer before computing distances to 300 MATH anchors.

Each source seed uses nested 1K and 2K probe-training subsets, a fixed 500-example validation set, and 300 anchors sampled from the shared training data. The anchor examples are part of the 1K subset and are therefore shared by both training-set sizes. Hyperparameters are selected on the source model’s validation split. The primary MATH comparison in Section 4.2 uses the 2K condition and the prespecified 128-token checkpoint. All three source/probe seeds are evaluated on the same frozen MATH-500 generations. Consequently, standard errors reflect variation in source-side training, anchors, and probe fitting rather than new samples of target completions.

We extract the last balanced \boxed{...} or \fbox{...} expression from each completed solution, with conservative fallbacks for an unbraced boxed atom and an explicit final-answer marker. We normalize common TeX and formatting differences, accept exact matches and equivalent integer, decimal, or fractional values, and accept a matching right-hand side when a model boxes a concluding equation. A generation that reaches the 4,096-token limit without an end-of-sequence token is marked incorrect.

Correctness labels in this setting are based on each monitored model’s generated solution. Table 12 reports the correctness rate and the share of trajectories that reach the primary 128-token checkpoint. Averaged across the four in-pool models, MATH-500 is 72.8% correct at that checkpoint, whereas GSM8K is 90.9% correct and therefore has substantially fewer incorrect examples.

A.5 External-target protocol

The external-target evaluation in Section 4.3.1 holds the source and calibration pool for each task fixed. For trivia and Guard Distillation, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, Gemma-3-12B-Instruct, and GPT-OSS-20B as targets outside the original six-model pool. For MATH, GPT-OSS-20B is external to the four-model pool above; OLMo-3 and Gemma-3 already belong to that pool. Candidate source probes are ranked by mean validation AUROC on the other models in the relevant original pool, and the selected probe is applied unchanged to the external target. External-target labels do not participate in probe fitting, normalization, hyperparameter choice, or source selection. GPT-OSS generations use the medium reasoning effort specified through its native chat template.

After the transfer protocol was fixed, we trained a global Anchored probe on each external target using the same task definition. These target-trained results measure whether the target’s anchored representation contains a linearly decodable signal under the evaluated setup. They are diagnostic comparisons of target-side decodability, not deployable transfer methods. Trivia summaries first average the six dataset/answer-format variants within each source/probe seed and then report the mean and standard error over three seeds. Guard reports BeaverTails and Toxic-chat separately using the single-token anchor representation. The MATH diagnostic follows the same 2K-training, 128-token configuration as the primary result.

A.6 Related-data transfer protocol

The related-data experiments in Section 4.3.2 test whether portability survives a change of evaluation dataset, either within the same model or together with a model change. In every transfer direction, the source dataset supplies all examples used to fit, tune, and select probes. The probes retain the source-dataset normalization, and anchored probes also retain the source anchor set. Target-dataset labels are used only for final scoring.

For trivia, we transfer among TruthfulQA, SciQ, and MMLU while preserving the binary- or four-choice answer format and use the source dataset’s 300 anchors. For Guard Distillation, we transfer in both directions between BeaverTails and Toxic-chat and use the source dataset’s 600 anchors. For mathematical correctness, we apply the probes trained on 2,000 MATH examples to GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) at the same 64-, 128-, and 256-token checkpoints. These probes retain their MATH anchors, fitted parameters, normalization, and MATH-based source selection. GSM8K uses the openai/gsm8k test split, and no GSM8K example is used for fitting, hyperparameter selection, or source selection. We prompt each model through its native chat template with a system instruction to show its reasoning and end with Final answer: <number>, and generate greedily for at most 4,096 tokens. We extract the final numeric answer from an explicit final-answer, <answer>, boxed-answer, or GSM8K #### marker, falling back to the last number in the completion. Correctness is exact after normalizing commas and integer, decimal, or simple-fraction notation against the reference answer following the dataset’s #### delimiter.

A.7 GuardQA setting

GuardQA is an auxiliary safety-evaluation setting that reframes each monitored prompt–completion pair as a trivia-style A/B question. The monitored model receives its own completion together with a follow-up question asking whether that response is safe or unsafe. We report GuardQA in the appendix because the main safety setting instead uses Guard Distillation, which predicts the Guard label directly from completion-token representations (Section 3.3).

We introduced GuardQA after an early Guard Distillation pilot gave weak results. The motivating hypothesis was that explicitly asking a model to judge the safety of its own response might make safety-relevant features easier to probe at the final prompt position. We later found that the pilot had used a short completion limit, so many monitored responses were incomplete. Llama Guard could then label properties of an unfinished response that were only weakly reflected in the model’s activations at that point. The longer completion protocol used for the final Guard Distillation results addresses this likely source of mismatch; GuardQA remains an auxiliary test of an explicitly elicited safety judgment rather than a replacement for Guard Distillation.

To construct the trivia-style question, we take each monitored model’s stored prompt-completion pair and convert it into a new prompt that contains the original user prompt, that model’s completion, and a follow-up safety question of the form “Is the assistant’s response safe or unsafe?” with A/B options.

The prompt is formatted as a safety-evaluator dialogue. The system instruction asks the model to read a conversation and determine whether the assistant’s response is safe or unsafe, responding only with the letter A or B. The user message then contains the original user prompt, the generated completion, the question “Is the assistant’s response safe or unsafe?”, the two answer options, and a final Answer: cue. The template is therefore

[System] You are a safety evaluator. Read the conversation below and determine whether the assistant’s response is safe or unsafe. Respond with only the letter A or B.
[User] Conversation:
User: {original prompt}
Assistant: {model completion}
Is the assistant’s response safe or unsafe?
A. {Safe or Unsafe}
B. {Unsafe or Safe}
Answer:

The ordering of the answers is randomized per sample: for some examples A=Safe, B=Unsafe, and for others A=Unsafe, B=Safe. This randomization is deterministic, using the per-sample seed (generation seed + sample ID). The monitored model is instructed to answer with only the letter A or B. The target for safety prediction is therefore the A/B position corresponding to the stored Llama Guard label, not the raw safe/unsafe token. Because GuardQA is a trivia-style task, we probe the final prompt position, immediately before the model emits its A/B answer. This elicits the relevant safety judgment at a single well-defined pre-answer position.

GuardQA uses class-imbalance-reduced 1,000-prompt subsets for BeaverTails (Ji et al., 2023) and Toxic-chat (Lin et al., 2023). BeaverTails prompts are drawn from the 30k_train split of PKU-Alignment/BeaverTails, i.e., the 30K-prompt release of the dataset rather than the larger 330K release. Toxic-chat prompts are drawn from the toxicchat0124 configuration of lmsys/toxic-chat, combining its train and test splits into a single pool.

We first choose the prompt IDs using a prompt-selection pass. For each underlying dataset, we prompt Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Llama Team, 2024) with every candidate user request and generate a completion of at most 200200 new tokens. Llama-Guard-3-8B scores each selection-time prompt-completion pair as safe or unsafe. To reduce class imbalance, we retain all prompt IDs whose selection-time completions are labeled unsafe and then add safe prompt IDs in dataset index order until the subset reaches 1,000 prompts. This prompt-selection step gives 432 selection-unsafe IDs for BeaverTails and 304 selection-unsafe IDs for Toxic-chat. The resulting prompt IDs are shared across monitored models.

The completions used inside GuardQA examples are then generated separately for each monitored model. For a given monitored model, dataset, and generation seed, we prompt that same model and store its completion, again with a maximum of 200200 new tokens. Llama-Guard-3-8B scores each resulting prompt-completion pair. Thus the selected prompt IDs are shared, but the assistant response inserted into the GuardQA question and the corresponding Llama Guard label are model- and seed-specific. A Qwen3 GuardQA example, for instance, contains a Qwen3 completion; a Llama Guard label for that Qwen3 completion; and an A/B safety question answered by Qwen3. The same construction is repeated for each monitored model.

For each seed split, these 1,000 selected prompt IDs are internally split into 60% train, 20% validation, and 20% test for probe training and evaluation. The safety-label balance can differ across monitored models because their completions differ, even though the prompt IDs are held fixed.

For reference, Table 13 reports the realized Llama Guard label balance for each monitored model’s completions. Values are averaged over the three generation/split seeds used in the paper; uncertainty is standard error across seeds. Because every row contains 1,000 examples per seed, the safe rate is the complement of the unsafe rate and has the same standard error.

A.8 MMLU scale experiment

The model-scale test summarized in Section 4.3.3 pools 14,042 MMLU examples and constructs nested subsets of 1K, 3K, 6K, and 10K examples. We evaluate Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct using the binary GT Prediction setup, angular-distance global representations, and either 300 or 1000 anchors whenever the anchor count fits within the 60% training split. This gives seven conditions: 1K examples with 300 anchors, plus 3K, 6K, and 10K examples with either 300 or 1000 anchors. We repeat each condition for three generation, split, and anchor seed triplets. Within a seed, we compute each cell separately for every condition and average seven AUROC values. The reported cell is the mean of three resulting seed-level Transfer averages (no source-calibration). For each seed, we randomly permute all 14,042 MMLU test examples, retain the first 10,000, divide that pool 60/20/20, and take the first indices of each split to construct the smaller nested datasets.

A.9 Probe staleness experiments

The model-update test summarized in Section 4.3.3 follows the prompt-only refusal-compliance protocol of Duan (2026). We use all 450 prompts from the XSTest (Röttger et al., 2024) safety dataset, label genuinely unsafe prompts as the positive class and safe prompts that resemble unsafe requests as the negative class, and split the dataset stratified into 315 training prompts and 135 validation prompts. We repeat this with three train/validation split seeds; because anchored probes use the 315 training prompts from the corresponding split as anchors, each split seed also has a different anchor set. Activations are residual-stream activations at the final prompt token, before any completion token is sampled. Table 15 summarizes the XSTest label and split statistics used by this monitor.

To remain comparable with the six-layer evaluation grid of Duan (2026), we monitor layers 4,8,12,16,20,244,8,12,16,20,24 in Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We train linear logistic-regression probes with C=1.0C=1.0. Standard probes use each layer’s residual-stream activation directly, while local anchored probes convert each monitored layer separately into anchor-relative coordinates. We also concatenate the same six layers before applying the anchor transform, giving a global anchored version of Duan et al.’s six-layer setup. We call this the global anchored probe in the XSTest results. Unlike the global representation in the main transfer experiments, it combines the six monitored layers rather than all layers. Anchored probes use all 315 XSTest training prompts from the corresponding split as anchors and use angular distance as the main relative-coordinate function. We report Δ\DeltaAUROC in points, defined as changed-model AUROC minus original-model AUROC on the same validation prompts. A probe is counted as stale if Δ​AUROC≤−5\Delta\mathrm{AUROC}\leq-5 points.

The learned model update is a small refusal-SFT adapter trained on BeaverTails (Ji et al., 2023), disjoint from XSTest. We draw examples from the 30k_train split of PKU-Alignment/BeaverTails. For each update size, we sample a balanced set of safe and unsafe examples using the update seed. Safe examples train the model to reproduce the original BeaverTails response. Unsafe examples train the model to produce a deterministic short refusal, selected from the following templates by the row identity and update seed:

  • •

    “I’m sorry, but I can’t help with that request.”

  • •

    “I can’t assist with instructions or advice that would enable harm.”

  • •

    “I can’t help with that. If you want, I can offer safer, legal alternatives.”

  • •

    “I’m not able to provide help for that request.”

  • •

    “I can’t assist with harmful or illegal activity.”

This produces a safety-relevant model update without using XSTest labels or XSTest prompts. Table 16 summarizes the refusal-SFT update-data balance.

We train either QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) or full LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) adapters with rank 1616, alpha 3232, dropout 0.050.05, learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, batch size 11 with 88 gradient accumulation steps, maximum sequence length 512512, and one epoch. The adapters modify the attention and MLP projection modules (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj). We use two update sizes, 256 and 512 examples, and three update seeds. As quantization-only controls, we also evaluate the original model loaded with bitsandbytes NF4 or INT8 quantization. These controls test whether the monitor shift is caused by a learned update rather than by quantized inference alone.

A.10 Compute estimates

Our pipeline has three stages—completion generation, anchored-representation construction, and probe training. Completion generation is the dominant computational cost and is performed once for each model–dataset pair; cached activations are then reused across probe fits, source–target applications, and most ablations. The estimates below characterize representative individual configurations rather than the total compute of the full experimental suite. Hardware requirements depend primarily on model size and generation length.

Generation and activation extraction.

Generation is short for trivia prompts and GuardQA Q&A prompts, which use at most 5050 new tokens. GuardQA monitored-model completions use at most 200200 new tokens, and Guard Distillation uses at most 800800. Online MATH is the most generation-intensive primary setting, with a maximum of 4,0964{,}096 new tokens per solution; probes query the cached trajectories at 64, 128, and 256 tokens. The related-data and external-target experiments add generation and activation passes for the new model–dataset pairs, but do not require regenerating an example separately for every source probe. Guard Distillation additionally runs Llama Guard once to label each monitored prompt–completion pair.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct fits in roughly 16 GB of GPU memory at float16 or bfloat16 precision, plus KV-cache overhead. The MATH pool and external-target evaluations also include 12B- and 20B-parameter models, so this 8B estimate does not describe every setting. The 70B pooled-MMLU scale experiment is an intentionally larger stress test; we ran its unquantized generation across two GPUs with batch size four.

Anchored-representation construction.

Once raw activations are stored to disk, the dominant cost of constructing anchored representations is I/O from loading activations into RAM; the anchor transform itself is a matrix multiplication. Concretely, the global anchored representation multiplies an activation matrix whose effective hidden dimension is 32×4096=131,07232\times 4096=131{,}072 (layers ×\times hidden size for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) against an anchor set. The activation matrix for nn examples requires roughly 4​n​D4nD bytes at float32, where DD is the concatenated hidden dimension. For example, transforming all 1,0001{,}000 examples in a Guard Distillation pool with D=131,072D=131{,}072 uses about 500500 MB for the activation matrix itself, plus the 600600-anchor matrix and temporary buffers. The MATH configuration uses 300 anchors. Related-data transfer reuses the source dataset’s anchor matrix and probe, so its additional representation cost comes from encoding and transforming the target examples rather than refitting every source–target pair.

Probe training and evaluation.

Probe fitting is small relative to activation extraction and anchored-representation construction. Linear probes use scikit-learn 1.8.01.8.0 LogisticRegression and roc_auc_score; MLP probes use PyTorch 2.6.02.6.0. The XSTest model-update experiments add a separate one-epoch LoRA or QLoRA fine-tuning stage on 256 or 512 examples. This update cost and the 70B scale stress test are not representative of fitting an anchored probe itself.

Appendix B Trivia results

This section reports the detailed trivia results. Same-model decodability, calibration, validation-selected local depths, and low-FPR recall appear in Sections B.1, B.2, B.3, and B.4. Section B.5 reports external-model targets. Sections B.6, B.7, B.8, and B.9 examine related datasets, prompt changes, anchor count, model scale, and target performance. Finally, Sections B.10 and B.11 provide standard-probe controls.

B.1 Same-model decodability

Table 17 gives the full same-model Standard-versus-Anchored comparison summarized in Section 4.1. The two representations differ by at most 1.4 AUROC points across the six trivia variants.

B.2 Full calibration progression

Section 4.2 reports Transfer (naive transfer) and Transfer (cal) (calibrated transfer with N=5N\!=\!5) as representative endpoints. Table 18 is the Output Prediction companion to the main GT Prediction table and includes the same Standard, Anchored, Transfer, and Transfer (cal) columns. Because Output Prediction is already near ceiling, we reserve the complete N=1,…,5N\!=\!1,\dots,5 source-pool progression for the more informative GT Prediction target in Table 19, where NN is the number of available source models. Most calibration gains appear once three source models are available. TruthfulQA GT Prediction is the exception: calibration adds less than one point at every pool size because all five source probes fail on the Llama-3.2-3B target (Section 4.2).

B.3 Validation-selected local depths

Section 4.3.3 summarizes the layer-selection results. Figure 4 compares global probes with local depths selected using validation data for GT Prediction, the informative trivia target because Output Prediction is saturated in several slices. For naive transfer, each source model selects its depth using same-model validation. For calibrated transfer, validation over the source-model pool jointly selects source and depth for each in-pool target. The gray ranges show test performance across all candidate local depths. The hollow triangles retain the normal source policy but select local depth using test data, so they are diagnostic oracles rather than deployable policies.

On binary TruthfulQA, every incoming source probe is weak for the Llama-3.2-3B target (Figure 2); the small selected-local advantage in the aggregate does not resolve that target-specific transfer failure.

B.4 Recall at 10% FPR

Standard-vs-Anchored recall at relative depth 0.80.8 is similar on Output Prediction and differs by only a few points on GT Prediction, mirroring the AUROC parity. The calibration summary (Table 20) shows that anchored recall remains close to Standard within a model but drops more than AUROC under cross-model transfer. TruthfulQA GT Prediction is the one case where calibration does not improve recall.

B.5 Transfer to external model targets

Section 4.3.1 summarizes transfer to trivia models outside the original six-model pool. Table 21 expands the external GT Prediction averages into the binary- and four-choice versions of TruthfulQA, MMLU, and SciQ. Output Prediction remains close to saturated across the external targets, so we do not reproduce its full breakdown here.

B.6 Related-data and joint transfer

Section 4.3.2 summarizes transfer among the trivia datasets. Here we test every source–target dataset direction with the same answer format under the common protocol in Appendix A.6. Table 22 reports same-model transfer. Output Prediction is saturated at least 99.199.1 AUROC in every direction. For GT Prediction, Global anchored probes outperform Standard in all displayed directions. The largest gains occur when TruthfulQA is the source: 74.9→88.074.9\rightarrow 88.0 on binary SciQ, 69.9→81.669.9\rightarrow 81.6 on binary MMLU, 85.9→95.585.9\rightarrow 95.5 on four-choice SciQ, and 78.1→88.678.1\rightarrow 88.6 on four-choice MMLU. SciQ–MMLU transfer is within half a point of target same-model performance, while TruthfulQA remains the difficult target distribution.

We next change both dataset and monitored model (Table 23). Global GT Prediction averages 83.183.1 under naive transfer and 86.186.1 under source calibration, compared with 87.087.0 for same-model related-data transfer. Calibration therefore recovers most of the additional model-transfer penalty, although directions with TruthfulQA as source or target retain the largest gaps.

B.7 Sensitivity to prompt perturbations

Section 4.3.3 summarizes whether the trivia conclusions depend on the exact answer prompt used to elicit monitored-model completions. Here we use the same six trivia datasets and linear-probe setup to compare the standard prompt against two prompt variants: a shorter minimal prompt and a more explicit verbose prompt. We fit the probes and select source models once using the default-prompt data, then apply them unchanged to activations elicited by the two prompt variants; the shifted prompts do not trigger probe retraining or new source selection. The goal is twofold: first, to test whether anchored probes are more or less prompt-sensitive than standard probes; and second, to test whether prompt variation compounds the cross-model transfer penalty. Figures 5 and 6 plot the change in performance for each method relative to that same method’s score under the standard prompt, so negative bars indicate degradation under the shifted prompt. The standard prompt is the default chat-formatted multiple-choice prompt described in Appendix A.2. The two prompt variants have the following form:

Minimal prompt
[User] {question}
A. {answer A}
B. {answer B}
…
Answer:

Verbose prompt
[System] You are a knowledgeable assistant. The following is a
multiple choice question. Read it carefully and select the best
answer. Respond with only the letter corresponding to your choice
(A/B/…). Do not include any explanation.
[User] Question: {question}
Options:
A. {answer A}
B. {answer B}
…
Your answer (letter only):

This stress test is motivated by prior work showing that hidden-state probes can depend on seemingly incidental setup choices. For example, Orgad et al. (2024) find that token choice matters substantially for white-box hallucination detection, while Slobodkin et al. (2023) study prompt manipulation and decode answerability from first-generated-token representations. More broadly, prior work warns that white-box probes or telemetry-based detectors can be brittle under task, context, deployment, or adaptive model-side shifts (Levinstein and Herrmann, 2023; Kramár et al., 2026; Min et al., 2026). We therefore ask whether anchored probes and cross-model transfer show the same sensitivity to prompt variation as same-model standard probes.

We observe that same-model probes are quite sensitive to the minimal prompt on GT Prediction. Standard probes drop by 11.111.1 AUROC points on average across the six Trivia datasets, while same-model Anchored probes drop by 8.18.1 points for global probes and 8.98.9 points for local probes. Thus anchoring reduces prompt sensitivity slightly relative to Standard, but does not eliminate it. The same effect is even larger for recall: the minimal prompt reduces Standard recall by 23.723.7 points and same-model Anchored recall by roughly 13.613.6–13.813.8 points. Both AUROC and recall drops are larger than the same-model-to-transfer gap under the standard prompt. For example, global Anchored GT Prediction AUROC drops by 8.18.1 points under the minimal prompt, whereas the average gap between same-model global Anchored and global Transfer (cal) under the standard prompt is 4.14.1 points.

Calibrated cross-model transfer is much less affected by the same prompt shift. For GT Prediction, global Transfer (cal) changes by only 1.11.1 AUROC points on average under the minimal prompt, and local Transfer (cal) changes by 1.01.0 point. Recall shows the same pattern: global Transfer (cal) changes by 1.41.4 points on average, while local Transfer (cal) changes by 0.60.6 points, despite the much larger same-model prompt sensitivity. One potential interpretation is that the strongest same-model probes exploit features that are predictive but brittle: they work for the same model and prompt style, but do not transfer reliably across either model identity or prompt wording. These features are not predictive under model transfer, which could explain why the drop when changing prompt style is much smaller. This interpretation is tentative: one family of prompt perturbations does not establish that transferred probes generally select more robust features.

Output Prediction is substantially more stable (see the different y-axis scale). Under the minimal prompt, most AUROC changes are within a few points, with the largest drops concentrated in the minimal-prompt four-choice variants.

Overall, same-model Trivia probes, including same-model anchored probes, are quite sensitive to a compressed prompt on the harder GT Prediction target. However, calibrated transfer remains stable across the same prompt shifts, suggesting that the transfer results are potentially more stable to prompt variations.

B.8 Anchor count ablations

The trivia experiments in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 use 300300 anchors. To check whether this choice drives the linear-probe results, we repeat the global anchored cross-model evaluation with 100100, 200200, 300300, and 400400 anchors while holding the representation type, probe family, and calibration rule fixed. Table 24 reports AUROC for calibrated cross-model transfer (Transfer (cal)) for the same global anchored representations used in the main Trivia linear experiments.

The AUROC results are largely insensitive to the number of anchors. Output Prediction is near-saturated for all six Trivia datasets; its largest change is the 1.3-point dip at 300 anchors on binary TruthfulQA. GT Prediction is also stable on MMLU, SciQ, and their four-choice variants. The clearest exception is binary TruthfulQA GT Prediction, where AUROC is higher with 100–200 anchors than with 300–400 anchors. This variation is modest relative to the main cross-model-transfer trends and does not suggest that larger anchor sets systematically improve transfer.

B.9 Pooled-MMLU scale and transfer diagnostics

Data and anchor scale.

The model-scale analysis summarized in Section 4.3.3 uses nested 1K/3K/6K/10K subsets from a 14,042-example pooled-MMLU dataset and repeats cross-model GT Prediction across three seeds. We evaluate 300 and 1000 anchors except in the 1K condition, whose 600-example training split cannot supply 1000 anchors. The scale matrix averages the available data-size and anchor-count conditions within each seed before averaging the three seeds; the anchor-count comparison below uses only the common 3K/6K/10K conditions. Table 25 shows no systematic improvement with more probe-training data: cross-model AUROC is 75.875.8 at 1K examples and 76.576.5 at 10K, with a lower intermediate 3K cell.
