On the common 3K/6K/10K grid, 300 anchors outperform 1000 (76.876.8 versus 74.774.7 cross-model AUROC), consistent with the Trivia anchor-count experiment in Appendix B.8.

Table 26 reports transfer across the same-family 1B/8B/70B ladder. It shows strong upward transfer into the 70B target and weak downward transfer into the 1B target. This scale experiment uses naive transfer and is separate from the six-model cross-family experiment in Section 4.2. The asymmetry repeats the weak-target pattern in Section 4.2. One possible interpretation is that features used by the 1B probe remain predictive in the larger models, whereas probes trained on larger models rely on richer distinctions that are absent or encoded differently in the 1B model.

Target-performance diagnostic.

Across the six main Trivia variants and six target models, target answer accuracy correlates strongly with mean incoming off-diagonal GT-transfer AUROC (Spearman ρ=0.976\rho=0.976, Pearson r=0.888r=0.888, n=36n=36 target–dataset cells). This extends the observed weak-target pattern from TruthfulQA to pooled MMLU. Because target accuracy requires labels, it is a retrospective correlate rather than a label-free pre-deployment signal. Figure 2 illustrates the pattern on binary TruthfulQA: transfer into Llama-3.2-3B remains near or below chance from every off-diagonal source, even though transfer into most other targets is strong. Within this dataset, target accuracy and mean incoming transfer have Spearman ρ=1.000\rho=1.000 (Pearson r=0.964r=0.964, n=6n=6); Llama-3.2-3B is lowest on both, with 55.8%55.8\% answer accuracy and 46.446.4 mean incoming AUROC.

B.10 Standard cross-model probe baseline

Section 4.2 argues that standard (non-anchored) probes cannot in general be applied directly across architectures. Here we test the same approach empirically for the one pair in our pool that shares both hidden dimension and layer count: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (both 4096-dim, 32 transformer layers). For this pair, a standard probe trained on one model can be applied directly to the other without any dimension mismatch.

For Trivia, standard transfer at relative depth 0.80.8 is weak and inconsistent: the average across cells is only 48.048.0 AUROC, versus 96.696.6 for the same-model standard baseline reported in Section 4.1. Under anchored global linear probes, mean cross-model AUROC rises from 48.048.0 to 94.094.0. Output Prediction remains at or above 9595 AUROC in both directions, showing that the anchored representation restores transferability that raw coordinates lack for this model pair (Tables 27 and 28).

B.11 All-layer standard probes

To separate the effect of anchor-relative coordinates from whole-network concatenation, we train standard probes (no anchoring) on the concatenated all-layer vector and compare them with single-layer standard probes across relative depths. At the prespecified standard-probe depth of 0.80.8, all-layer standard probes usually match a single-layer standard probe. This indicates that all-layer concatenation may also, in principle, provide a strong standard linear probing default. However, the resulting feature vector is quite large, at (num_layers×hidden_dim)(\texttt{num\_layers}\times\texttt{hidden\_dim}), and this may complicate training especially for non-linear probes. The additional benefit of the global anchored representation is fixing the feature dimension to the number of anchors.

For Trivia linear probes, the all-layer and depth-0.80.8 single-layer standard probes have similar AUROC (Tables 29 and 30). The depth sweep in Figure 7 shows that the all-layer standard probe mainly helps relative to shallow single-layer probes.

Appendix C Guard Distillation results

This section expands the Guard Distillation results. The calibration progression and low-FPR recall results appear in Sections C.1, C.2. Section C.3 reports external model targets. The related-data transfer results appear in Section C.4. Sections  C.5, C.6, and C.7 examine anchor-token aggregation, anchor coverage, and local-depth selection. Probe-design checks cover class balancing and attention pooling in Sections  C.8 and C.9. Section C.10 reports relational evidence; Section C.11 evaluates MLP probes. Sections C.12, C.13, and C.14 provide additional cross-model controls.

C.1 Full calibration progression

Section 4.2 reports Transfer (naive transfer) and Transfer (cal) (calibrated transfer with N=5N\!=\!5) as representative endpoints. Table 31 reports the complete N=1,…,5N\!=\!1,\dots,5 progression alongside the Anchored same-model column for Guard Distillation linear probes with single-token anchors, where NN is the number of available source models. Transfer reaches 81.181.1 AUROC on BeaverTails and 81.681.6 on Toxic-chat; Transfer (cal) improves both datasets, reaching 86.486.4 on BeaverTails and 83.683.6 on Toxic-chat. Relative to chance, Transfer (cal) preserves 81.1%81.1\% and 89.6%89.6\% of same-model Anchored performance, respectively.

C.2 Recall at 10% FPR

Low-FPR recall retains the AUROC ordering but has larger gaps between same-model and transferred probes. With single-token anchors, Table 32 shows that same-model Standard and Anchored recall are close: Anchored reaches 82.082.0 on BeaverTails and 65.965.9 on Toxic-chat, compared with 86.086.0 and 68.668.6 for the single-layer Standard probe at relative depth 0.80.8. The full calibration progression in Table 33 shows that naive Transfer drops to 55.455.4 and 47.747.7, respectively, while Transfer (cal) improves to 63.563.5 on BeaverTails and 53.053.0 on Toxic-chat. Thus calibration remains useful at low FPR, especially on BeaverTails, but the recall metric exposes more cross-model fragility than AUROC.

C.3 Transfer to external model targets

Section 4.3.1 summarizes transfer to Guard Distillation targets outside the original six-model pool. Table 34 separates BeaverTails and Toxic-chat and reports their unsafe-completion rates. Toxic-chat provides the more stable external-target test: all seed-level AUROCs are defined and calibrated transfer remains strongest for OLMo-3. BeaverTails has only 1.0–4.8% unsafe completions across the three external models. One OLMo-3 test seed contains no unsafe example, so both its target-trained and transferred AUROC are undefined; the reported OLMo-3 BeaverTails means use the other two seeds. This imbalance makes BeaverTails a demanding, high-uncertainty test, while the lower GPT-OSS and Gemma-3 point estimates show that low prevalence is not the only relevant source of transfer error.

C.4 Related-data and joint transfer

Section 4.3.2 summarizes transfer between BeaverTails and Toxic-chat. Here we report both directions, first for the same monitored model and then while also changing model identity, using the common protocol in Appendix A.6. Hidden-state detectors can be brittle under such distribution shifts (Orgad et al., 2024; Levinstein and Herrmann, 2023; Kramár et al., 2026; Min et al., 2026).

Table 35 reports the same-model result. Averaged over directions, Standard, Global, and Local reach 78.378.3, 77.977.9, and 77.977.9 AUROC. This aggregate hides a strong asymmetry: Global reaches 70.270.2 from BeaverTails to Toxic-chat but 85.585.5 in the reverse direction. Anchoring therefore roughly matches Standard on average but does not make this distribution shift uniformly robust.

Changing both dataset and model further reduces performance (Table 36). Global Transfer reaches 64.364.3/75.875.8 by direction and 70.170.1 overall; source calibration raises the reverse direction to 79.679.6 but changes the weak direction only to 65.165.1, for 72.472.4 overall. Calibration therefore does not close the directional gap.

C.5 Anchor-aggregation sensitivity

We repeat both same-model related-data transfer and joint model-and-dataset transfer with mean-token anchors, which average each anchor completion’s token representations before computing anchor-relative features. The anchor index still refers to the same prompt across models, but the corresponding vector now depends on each model’s generated completion. This comparison tests whether prompt-indexed relational structure can remain useful even when exact anchor tokens are not shared.

When training and evaluating on the same dataset, mean-token anchors change same-model AUROC by at most 1.11.1 points and calibrated transfer by at most 2.72.7 points. Under same-model related-data transfer, they raise the Global/Local averages from 77.977.9/77.977.9 to 80.080.0/80.680.6 (Table 37). When both dataset and model change, switching to mean-token anchors has mixed effects: calibrated Global improves from 72.472.4 to 75.075.0 overall, while naive Global falls from 70.170.1 to 65.865.8 (Table 38). Mean-token anchors are therefore a useful sensitivity result, not a uniformly better replacement for the single-token-anchor baseline.

C.6 Anchor coverage and mixed-anchor mitigation

The weak BeaverTails→\rightarrowToxic-chat direction also has poorer label-free anchor coverage: its mean nearest-anchor angular distance is 1.2091.209, versus 1.1821.182 in the reverse direction, while same-model degradation is 17.317.3 versus 9.39.3 points. Across all applications this association is only moderate; nearest-anchor distance tracks the directional difference here but is not an established general predictor.

We test a coverage-oriented intervention using an unlabeled 50/50 anchor pool from both datasets. In the mean-token setting, mixed global anchors narrow the naive direction gap from 9.69.6 to 1.91.9 points, but leave average naive AUROC similar and reduce calibrated average AUROC from 75.075.0 to 70.470.4. They do improve low-FPR recall in the weak direction, from 17.917.9 to 28.728.7 naively and from 24.924.9 to 35.535.5 after calibration. Mixed anchors thus alter the failure pattern and improve weak-direction coverage; they do not uniformly improve AUROC or solve the underlying shift (Table 39).

Local mixed-anchor results are less stable and sometimes reverse the directional imbalance. Mixed anchors therefore do not provide a consistently better response to the data shift (Table 40).

C.7 Validation-selected local depths

Figure 8 compares local-depth selection with the global representation for both single-token and mean-token anchors. For same-model evaluation, each model and seed selects a depth using its own validation split. For naive transfer, each source selects its depth using source-model validation. For calibrated transfer, source-pool validation jointly selects source and depth for each in-pool target. All reported values are then evaluated on test data; only the hollow-triangle oracle uses test AUROC to choose depth.

For the single-token comparison summarized in Section 4.3.3, validation-based depth selection improves calibrated local transfer from 85.185.1 to 86.486.4 AUROC on BeaverTails and from 80.480.4 to 82.082.0 on Toxic-chat. The selected local probe ties global on BeaverTails and trails it on Toxic-chat (82.082.0 versus 83.683.6). Across both anchor constructions, joint source–depth validation often improves on fixed depth 0.80.8, but does not consistently realize the stronger local result visible to the test oracle. Global anchoring is therefore the more reliable depth-free choice under the available validation protocol.

C.8 Class balancing ablation

We also check whether class balancing is useful for linear Guard Distillation probes. In particular, we run mean-token-anchor global probes with class balancing. Table 41 shows that class balancing is not an across-the-board improvement. It slightly improves BeaverTails same-model AUROC and recall, but worsens BeaverTails naive-transfer AUROC and recall. On Toxic-chat, class balancing is worse in both same-model and transfer comparisons for both metrics. Thus despite the heavy imbalance in the Guard Distillation data (Table 9), the linear Guard results do not suggest that class weighting is generally beneficial.

C.9 Sequence probing with attention probes

Because the Guard Distillation probes aggregate completion-token representations, we also test whether a learned attention-pooling probe can improve over fixed mean pooling. This is plausible because attention can, in principle, focus on especially informative generated tokens rather than averaging over the full completion. Like the class-balancing check above, this diagnostic uses the mean-token-anchor variant rather than the main single-token-anchor baseline. The diagnostic attention probe uses the same global anchored feature construction and mean-token anchors as the fixed linear/mean-token reference: 600600 sampled anchors, angular-distance relative coordinates, completion-token relative activations, and the same six monitored models and Guard datasets. Architecturally, it is a single-head attention-pooling probe: a learned linear score is applied to each completion-token feature vector, a softmax pools tokens into one weighted feature vector, and a linear binary classifier predicts the Guard label. We train these probes in PyTorch with AdamW, learning rate 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 10−210^{-2}, batch size 6464, and up to 2020 epochs with validation-loss early stopping with patience 33.

In diagnostic runs, unbalanced attention pooling is consistently worse than a matched linear probe with mean pooling, with large AUROC gaps for both same-model Anchored evaluations and cross-model Transfer on both Guard datasets.

We also try class balancing as a diagnostic for why the unbalanced attention probe underperforms. The motivation is that Guard labels are skewed, so an unbalanced training objective can obtain reasonable loss or accuracy by emphasizing the majority class and underweighting the rarer safety violations. This concern is stronger for attention than for the linear/mean probes because attention must also learn which tokens to pool; if minority-class evidence is rare, the pooling rule can receive little pressure to attend to those tokens. Class balancing helps substantially, suggesting that label skew is a real optimization issue for learned attention pooling. This contrasts with the fixed linear/mean probes in Section C.8, where class balancing does not help overall and tends to hurt transfer. Even after balancing, however, attention remains below the linear/mean reference overall: the BeaverTails transfer AUROC gap is small, but same-model performance, Toxic-chat transfer, and recall at 0.10.1 FPR remain clearly weaker.

As an additional regularization check, we run the class-balanced attention diagnostic with AdamW weight decay set to 10−110^{-1} instead of 10−210^{-2}, while keeping the same AUROC checkpoint selection. This stronger regularization gives small AUROC gains and improves same-model low-FPR recall, especially on BeaverTails, but does not close the gap to the linear/mean reference. BeaverTails transfer AUROC is close, but same-model performance, Toxic-chat transfer, and low-FPR recall still lag.

Completion length is a consistent diagnostic difference, but the detailed pattern depends on the dataset and regularization setting. In BeaverTails transfer, attention is closest to linear/mean on short completions and remains substantially worse on long completions; class balancing and stronger weight decay reduce this long-completion gap but do not remove it. Toxic-chat also shows length sensitivity, though the largest remaining gap after balancing is on middle-length completions rather than the longest completions, and stronger regularization mostly preserves that pattern. A similar pattern applies to the same-model setting: on same-model BeaverTails evaluations, balanced attention is close to linear/mean on short completions but substantially worse on longer completions, including under stronger regularization.

In the tested configurations, attention pooling is a worse inductive bias for Guard Distillation relative-token sequences, even after reducing the label-imbalance issue. This is not a generic failure of the attention architecture: for the Standard same-model probing baseline, attention is close to linear/mean in AUROC and at low FPR. The observed underperformance is thus specific to the combination of attention pooling and anchored features in this experiment; determining whether data volume, regularization, or another factor causes the gap requires further study.

C.10 Anchor correspondence and relational controls

Section 4.3.3 summarizes our tests of how closely anchor representations must correspond across models. Here we ask whether different models organize the shared anchor examples similarly enough for their identities to be recovered from relational geometry alone. We hide the anchor correspondence and give the matching procedure only the two anchor-to-anchor distance matrices. Without prompt content or a shared activation basis, the matcher can identify an anchor only through its pattern of distances to the other anchors. Above-chance recovery therefore indicates that these relational patterns are partly preserved across models. Table 42 summarizes the aggregate result: graph matching recovers 20.7% of hidden identities, compared with 0.16% for random one-to-one mappings. Applying the source probe after this recovered mapping yields 79.0 AUROC, versus 54.8 for random mappings and 83.2 with known prompt correspondence. The recovered correspondence is therefore also functionally useful. Normal monitor deployment uses known anchor identities and does not require correspondence recovery.

Blinded recovery protocol.

For each model pair, we construct a 600×600600\times 600 matrix of angular distances among the Guard anchors. The target anchor order is randomized. The matching procedure receives only the source and reordered target matrices. It has no access to the anchor prompts, hidden correspondence, labels, fitted probe, validation set, or test set.

We first describe each anchor by 64 quantiles of its distances to the other anchors. These summaries are invariant to the order of the remaining anchors. A linear assignment gives an initial one-to-one mapping. We refine the mapping by maximizing agreement between all pairwise distances. The refinement uses the initial assignment, a uniform initialization, and two seeded randomized initializations. We select the mapping with the highest geometric objective.

One BeaverTails seed-1 condition served as the development pilot for the two-stage procedure, the 64-quantile fingerprint, and the graph-matching initializations. These choices were then frozen before evaluation across BeaverTails and Toxic-chat, three seed configurations, and four prespecified model pairs. Two pairs are within the Llama or Qwen2.5 families. Two cross-family pairs compare Llama-3.1-8B with Mistral-7B or Qwen2.5-7B. Each of the 24 pair conditions is evaluated in both transfer directions and compared with 20 random one-to-one mappings.

Table 43 shows substantial variation across model-pair scope. Exact recovery reaches 20.6% for same-family BeaverTails pairs and 46.8% for same-family Toxic-chat pairs. The corresponding cross-family values are 10.3% and 5.3%. Cross-family recovery remains above the random expectation. Its functional value depends strongly on the dataset. Graph-mapped AUROC is 78.9 on the BeaverTails cross-family pairs and 68.8 on the Toxic-chat cross-family pairs.

Known prompt identity is a correspondence control. Its mean AUROC is higher than graph matching overall. Graph matching exceeds it in 12 of the 48 directions. Graph matching directly optimizes agreement between the two anchor graphs and can occasionally find a task-favorable permutation. Its in-sample edge agreement should therefore not be treated as an independent outcome. Exact hidden-identity recovery and test-set probe transfer provide the independent evaluations.

Probe-weighted recovery weights every correctly mapped anchor by the absolute coefficient assigned to that source coordinate, then divides by the total absolute coefficient weight. Its similarity to exact recovery indicates that the current matcher does not preferentially recover the most heavily weighted probe coordinates. Chance-corrected retention is (AUROCtransfer−0.5)/(AUROCsame​-​model−0.5)(\mathrm{AUROC}_{\mathrm{transfer}}-0.5)/(\mathrm{AUROC}_{\mathrm{same\text{-}model}}-0.5).

Coordinate-permutation control.

We also test whether a frozen source probe depends on the ordering of the known anchor coordinates. For every directed source–target pair among the six main models, we derange 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of the target coordinates. Each nonzero fraction uses 20 deterministic permutations. Mean AUROC declines from 0.812 to 0.524 on BeaverTails and from 0.816 to 0.582 on Toxic-chat as the permuted fraction increases from 0% to 100%. A coordinated control applies the same permutation to target features, scaler statistics, and probe coefficients. It reproduces the original probabilities to numerical precision.

This control confirms that transfer uses matched anchor indexing. Its interpretation is limited because any coordinate-sensitive classifier should degrade when feature values are paired with the wrong fitted coefficients. We therefore treat it as an implementation and indexing check.

Frame congruence and transfer.

Finally, we ask whether a scalar measure of agreement between matched anchor frames predicts functional transfer. This analysis contains 90 unordered model-pair, dataset, and seed conditions. Spearman correlation between corresponding anchor-graph edges is 0.146 with mean bidirectional AUROC, 0.208 with mean bidirectional chance-corrected retention, and 0.273 with minimum bidirectional retention. Block-bootstrap 95% intervals are [−0.055,0.256][-0.055,0.256], [0.048,0.261][0.048,0.261], and [0.112,0.353][0.112,0.353], respectively.

The relationship varies by dataset. For mean retention, the correlation is 0.224 on BeaverTails and −0.015-0.015 on Toxic-chat. Alignment measures computed on validation examples are also mixed. Matched-profile correlation and linear CKA do not reliably predict transfer. A modest pooled RSA association is driven by BeaverTails. The dataset-dependent and mostly null associations provide no reliable label-free scalar predictor for an individual transfer. They motivate the constructive recovery test and bound the interpretation of geometric agreement.

C.11 MLP probes

We next ask whether the global anchored representation also supports nonlinear probes. We use an MLP with 6464 hidden units, no dropout, weight decay 0.0010.001, no class weighting, and mean-token completion aggregation. These MLP probes also use mean-token anchors, whereas the linear Guard comparison in Section 4.2 uses single-token anchors. We optimize with Adam at learning rate 10−310^{-3} and batch size 6464 for at most 50 epochs. Training stops after five epochs without improvement in validation loss, and we restore the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss. Table 44 shows same-model performance for standard non-anchored probes and global anchored probes. The global MLP remains below the linear global probe in same-model AUROC, but retains strong performance: 92.292.2 AUROC on BeaverTails and 83.183.1 on Toxic-chat. The standard MLP baseline is also below the standard linear probe, so the MLP results should be read as a nonlinear stress test rather than a replacement for the linear Guard probe.

With source-training normalization, however, cross-model MLP transfer is poor. We therefore test whether the nonlinear probe is sensitive to differences in feature scaling between source and target models.

The relevant implementation detail is feature normalization. Like most probe-training pipelines, our probes normalize features before fitting the classifier. In the standard same-model setting, and in most of our linear transfer experiments, this normalization uses the feature mean and standard deviation estimated on the source model’s probe-training split. For cross-model transfer, however, those source-model statistics need not match the target model’s anchored feature distribution. This mismatch is mild for the linear Guard probes: in the spot check in Table 47, replacing source-train normalization by target-anchor normalization changes cross-model AUROC by at most about one point. For the MLP, source-normalized transfer produces saturated scores and poor performance. We therefore evaluate a target-anchor normalization strategy. At application time, we normalize the target model’s anchored features using the mean and standard deviation of that target model’s anchor-example features, rather than the source model’s training examples. This uses no target Guard labels and no target train/validation/test examples; it only reuses the anchor prompts that are already required to construct the anchored representation.

Cross-model transfer is more nuanced. Table 45 shows that target-anchor-normalized naive single-source transfer reaches 76.576.5 AUROC on BeaverTails and 78.078.0 on Toxic-chat. On BeaverTails, this is slightly above the linear global-probe naive transfer result (75.075.0 AUROC), but the difference is small relative to run-to-run uncertainty; on Toxic-chat, it remains below linear. Canonical source selection by validation AUROC gives only modest additional gains for this MLP: Transfer (cal) reaches 78.778.7 AUROC on BeaverTails and 78.578.5 on Toxic-chat. Most of the improvement therefore comes from changing the normalization rather than from source selection.

At low false-positive rates, the target-anchor-normalized MLP still trails the linear Guard probe. Transfer (cal) reaches 46.046.0 R@0.1FPR on BeaverTails and 41.741.7 on Toxic-chat. Thus target-anchor normalization substantially reduces the source-normalized MLP failure, but it does not make the MLP competitive with the linear Guard probe on recall (Table 46).

Target-anchor normalization

Figure 9 compares source-training and target-anchor normalization. With source-training normalization, naive cross-model AUROC averages only 57.757.7 on BeaverTails and 62.962.9 on Toxic-chat. Replacing source normalization by target-anchor normalization raises this to 76.576.5 and 78.078.0, respectively. The large gap between source-normalized and target-anchor-normalized MLP transfer suggests that the nonlinear probe is sensitive to cross-model differences in the scale of anchor-relative features, rather than primarily to label calibration. Target-anchor normalization mitigates the observed failure using only unlabeled anchor examples from the target model. For R@0.1FPR, target-anchor normalization also improves the MLP relative to its source-normalized version, but only recovers it from a collapsed baseline: after normalization, the MLP still remains below or roughly tied with the linear global probe.

Target-anchor normalization is much less important for linear probes in this experiment. Table 47 shows a single-seed Guard linear spot check: target-anchor normalization changes AUROC by at most about one point, and it does not improve the R@0.1FPR metric in this spot check. This supports a practical distinction: target-anchor normalization is useful for avoiding the source-normalized MLP transfer failure, especially in AUROC, but it is not a general recipe for improving low-FPR recall.

Alternative MLP configurations

We sweep a small set of target-anchor-normalized MLP regularization and architecture variants. Table 48 includes the default MLP and four variants with weight decay 0.010.01, 3232 or 6464 hidden units, with or without dropout. For compactness, table columns use h64/h32 for hidden size, d0.0/d0.1 for dropout probability, and wd for weight decay. The regularized variants move naive transfer only modestly, so we retain the default MLP with 6464 hidden units for the baseline and normalization comparisons in this appendix. All five target-anchor-normalized MLP variants have similar AUROC and retain the same BeaverTails-versus-Toxic-chat ordering.

We also test class-balanced training for the 6464-hidden-unit, no-dropout architecture. Table 49 shows that it does not help: the default AUROC values repeat the 6464-hidden-unit, no-dropout column in Table 48, and class balancing does not improve either AUROC or R@0.1FPR. We therefore use no class weighting in every default-MLP comparison reported here.

C.12 Standard cross-model probe baseline

We apply Guard Distillation linear probes directly between Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, the two models with matching hidden size and layer count. Table 50 shows that direct standard-probe transfer at relative depth 0.80.8 is near chance and averages 49.749.7 AUROC across the two Guard datasets, both directions, and three seeds. Thus, even for a hidden-size- and layer-count-matched model pair, raw-coordinate Guard Distillation probes do not reliably transfer across models.

Table 51 reports global anchored linear probes for the same model pair. Anchoring gives large gains on three of the four cells, although BeaverTails Mistral→\toLlama remains weak (42.942.9 AUROC). Figure 10 shows that this is part of a broader directed pattern: on BeaverTails, the Mistral-source column is weak for most non-self targets, while several other source columns transfer well. Mistral’s BeaverTails completions also have the highest unsafe rate (12.2%12.2\%, versus 2.02.0–6.6%6.6\% for other monitored models; Table 9). This coincident distributional difference does not explain the AUROC gap by itself, because AUROC is insensitive to class prevalence.

C.13 All-layer standard probes

To separate the effect of anchor-relative coordinates from whole-network concatenation, we train standard probes (no anchoring) on the concatenated all-layer vector and compare them with single-layer standard probes across relative depths.

Guard linear.

For Guard linear probes, the all-layer standard probe (C=0.1C=0.1) performs close to the single-layer standard probe at depth 0.80.8 (Table 52; Figure 11, left). It is slightly lower on BeaverTails (96.196.1 vs. 96.596.5 AUROC) and slightly higher on Toxic-chat (89.289.2 vs. 88.688.6 AUROC). Thus the Guard linear result matches the Trivia pattern: all-layer standard probes are competitive with strong single-layer standard probes.

Guard MLP.

For Guard MLP standard probes, the all-layer absolute representation performs worse than the depth-0.80.8 single-layer representation. The single-layer MLP-64 probe outperforms the all-layer MLP-64 probe on both Guard datasets (92.592.5 vs. 84.784.7 AUROC on BeaverTails and 83.583.5 vs. 72.972.9 on Toxic-chat). One possible explanation is that the higher-dimensional all-layer input needs different regularization, but this experiment does not isolate the cause. The global anchored representation has a fixed feature dimension. Its all-layer result remains competitive with the single-layer probe in the MLP setting (Table 53; Figure 11, right).

C.14 Model family analysis

We next ask whether cross-model transfer is correlated with model family or size. This diagnostic uses naive single-source Transfer. It exposes the directed source–target structure that calibration averages over.

For each grouping rule, we partition the six models into groups and average directed source–target transfer pairs according to whether the source and target fall in the same group or in different groups. The exact-family split compares pairs within the same named family (for example, Qwen2.5-to-Qwen2.5) against all other directed pairs. The coarser split compares Llama+Mistral against Qwen. The size split compares 7/87/8B models against 3/43/4B models. A grouping would be explanatory if the same-group and different-group columns showed a large, consistent gap. We also report each model’s average behavior as a target and as a source. “As target” averages probes trained on all other models and evaluated on that model. “As source” averages that model’s probe evaluated on all other models.

For Guard linear probes, family and size groupings show limited separation. Exact-family pairs are somewhat higher than different-family pairs (84.984.9 vs. 80.880.8 AUROC). The coarser Llama+Mistral/Qwen split differs by 0.30.3 points (81.281.2 vs. 81.581.5), and the size split is exactly tied at the reported precision (81.481.4 vs. 81.481.4; Table 54). Directional source–target differences are larger. Qwen2.5-3B is the weakest target at 71.371.3 AUROC, with a 16.716.7 point gap to same-model Anchored. Mistral-7B is the weakest source at 66.466.4 AUROC and is a strong target (Table 55). Thus the Guard result mirrors the broader conclusion: transfer depends more on which representation is used as source or target than on a simple family or size match.

Appendix D Online mathematical correctness results

This section reports calibration and depth-selection results for online MATH monitoring in Section D.1, low-FPR recall in Section D.2, the external GPT-OSS target in Section D.3, and related-data transfer to GSM8K in Section D.4.

D.1 Calibration and depth selection

Section 4.2 reports the primary 2K result at 128 tokens. Table 56 extends this comparison across all three generation checkpoints and available source-pool sizes. Global transfer improves as the source pool grows at every checkpoint. At 128 tokens, mean single-source transfer reaches 75.2 AUROC, calibration among two available sources reaches 76.8, and calibration among all three reaches 78.0.

We also ask whether validation can identify a useful local depth. Figure 12 compares the global probe with local probes on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-3-7B, and Gemma-3-12B at the 128-token checkpoint. The two panels use nested 1K and 2K source-training sets. At each local depth, source-pool validation selects a source model; the orange diamond jointly selects one source–depth pair using the same validation data. Neither deployable policy uses MATH-500 test labels. The selected local and global policies are close at both training sizes, extending the layer-selection result in Section 4.3.3: the MATH comparison does not provide a consistent reason to prefer local depth selection.

D.2 Low-FPR recall

Table 57 reports R@0.1FPR for the 128-token MATH-500 and GSM8K comparisons. On MATH-500, global anchoring raises same-model recall from 40.740.7 to 49.149.1, while calibrated global transfer reaches 38.738.7 and validation-selected local transfer reaches 44.744.7. Under the combined model-and-data shift to GSM8K, calibrated global transfer reaches 30.830.8, compared with 18.318.3 for the same-model Standard probe. Low-FPR recall therefore follows the main AUROC pattern: transfer trails the same-model Anchored probe but remains competitive with the Standard baseline.

D.3 Transfer to an external model target

Section 4.3.1 summarizes transfer to the external GPT-OSS MATH target. Table 58 reports the post-hoc target-trained diagnostic alongside calibrated transfer. Correctness is linearly decodable in GPT-OSS at both source-training sizes, whereas the source-trained decision rule remains near chance. This comparison diagnoses the MATH transfer failure; target-trained probes do not enter source selection or the transfer procedure.

D.4 Related-data transfer

Section 4.3.2 summarizes joint transfer from MATH to GSM8K. We evaluate the MATH-trained probes on GSM8K at the 128-token checkpoint under the protocol in Appendix A.6. Table 59 separates the effect of changing the data from the additional effect of changing the model. Within the same model, global anchored probes reach 75.3 AUROC, compared with 63.0 for standard probes. Calibrated transfer across both model and dataset reaches 70.5.

Appendix E XSTest probe staleness

This section first measures how probes trained on the original model behave after quantization and refusal fine-tuning (Section E.1). It then compares angular distance with cosine similarity (Section E.2) and whether re-encoding anchors after the model update improves robustness (Section E.3).

E.1 Staleness after model updates

Activation monitors are often trained once and then kept fixed while the model being monitored is updated. This creates a staleness risk: the updated model may still encode the relevant safety distinction, but the old probe may no longer read it out reliably. We test whether anchored representations reduce this failure mode. Following Duan (2026), we study the Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct models used in their staleness experiments. We train standard and anchored probes to predict whether an XSTest prompt is unsafe (Röttger et al., 2024); the dataset contains unsafe prompts and safe prompts that resemble unsafe prompts. We fit the probes on the original model checkpoints, freeze them, and evaluate them after either quantization-only changes or small refusal-SFT updates based on BeaverTails. The global anchored probe concatenates the six layers monitored by Duan (2026) before applying the anchor transform. Section 4.3.3 summarizes the main result; full implementation details are in Appendix A.9.

Table 60 isolates quantized inference before considering learned adapters. On Qwen2.5-7B, quantization changes all mean AUROCs by less than half a point. On Qwen2.5-3B, standard probes degrade more visibly, especially under NF4, but the shift is concentrated in one monitored layer. Global anchored probes remove almost all of this quantization sensitivity: their mean drop is at most 0.40.4 points and no global probe crosses the stale threshold.

Learned updates create much larger shifts (Table 61). On Qwen2.5-3B, standard probes lose roughly 88–1010 AUROC points across QLoRA and LoRA updates. On Qwen2.5-7B, QLoRA is milder but still reaches the stale threshold at 512 examples, while the 256-example full-LoRA update drops standard probes by 8.18.1 points. Like Duan (2026), we find that learned safety fine-tuning affects probe performance much more than quantization alone.

Global anchored probes provide a strong mitigation for the performance drop. For Qwen2.5-7B, no global probe is stale in any updated setting, and the mean drop remains between 0.10.1 and 1.21.2 points. For Qwen2.5-3B, global anchored probes improve substantially over standard probes: their mean drop stays below the 55-point stale magnitude in every setting. Local anchored probes also improve over standard probes on 3B, but worsen staleness on 7B.

Overall, standard probes show clear probe staleness after refusal fine-tuning, while quantized inference alone does not produce a comparable drop. Global anchored representations substantially reduce staleness under the tested LoRA and QLoRA updates.

E.2 Relative-coordinate function

The XSTest result summarized in Section 4.3.3 uses angular distance for anchored representations. We ablate the function used to construct anchored features by comparing angular distance to cosine similarity. Table 62 compares the pre-update probe scores. The two choices are close before any update, but angular distance is slightly better for local anchored probes on both models and slightly better for the 3B global anchored probe. In either case, global anchored probes match or exceed the best layer-averaged standard result before model updates.

Cosine-similarity staleness

Cosine-similarity probes reproduce the angular-distance ordering under quantization-only changes (Table 63): 7B changes little, 3B standard probes show a modest drop, and global anchored probes remove nearly all of the quantization sensitivity.

Under learned updates (Table 64), cosine similarity again shows that global anchored probes mitigate probe staleness, while local anchored probes are model-dependent. Cosine global anchored probes are less robust than their angular-distance counterparts. On 3B, cosine global drops remain around 66–88 points, whereas angular-distance global drops are around 33–44 points. On 7B, cosine global probes remain stable relative to standard probes, but their drops are also larger than with angular distance. Cosine similarity therefore still mitigates global-probe staleness, but angular distance is more robust for this task.

E.3 Re-encoding anchors after model updates

The angular-distance and cosine results above keep each original model’s anchor encodings fixed after the monitored model changes. A natural alternative is to re-encode the same anchor prompts with the updated model before computing anchored representations. This could help if the model update moves anchor prompts and evaluation prompts in a coherent way: similarities between updated evaluation prompts and updated anchors might then resemble the original-model similarity coordinates better than similarities between updated evaluation prompts and original-model anchors. Under this cancellation hypothesis, updated-anchor encodings should be more stable than original-anchor encodings.

Table 65 shows a mixed result for angular distance. Updated anchors often help local anchored probes, especially on Qwen2.5-7B, but these local probes still do not match the robustness of global anchored probes. For global anchored probes, updated anchors are close to original anchors in some rows, but they are worse in several 512-example settings. The hypothesized cancellation effect is therefore partially visible for local anchored features, but it is not the driver of the strongest mitigation.

Cosine similarity also fails to make updated-anchor encoding consistently beneficial (Table 66). Updated anchors sometimes help local anchored probes, especially for 3B LoRA, but they also hurt local probes under QLoRA and do not fix the poor 7B local results. For global anchored probes, updated anchors are close to original anchors in some rows, but they are substantially worse in several settings, including the 512-example 3B updates. Across both relative-coordinate functions, re-encoding anchors after the model update is therefore not a reliable replacement for the fixed anchor coordinate system used by probes trained before the model update.

Appendix F GuardQA results

This section reports same-model performance and calibrated transfer in Sections F.1 and F.2, followed by low-FPR recall in Section F.3. Section F.4 tests MLP width, local-depth selection, and anchor count; Sections F.5 and F.6 report linear-probe and standard cross-model controls.

F.1 Same-model summary

GuardQA is an auxiliary safety-evaluation setting that poses a trivia-style A/B question about the monitored model’s own completion. It elicits an explicit safety judgment at the final prompt position, complementing the completion-token Guard Distillation monitor defined in Section 3.3. Table 67 reports the same-model AUROC comparison for the GuardQA MLP setting (h=64h\!=\!64, 300300 anchors). Section F.2 reports cross-model transfer and its full calibration progression.

F.2 Full calibration progression

Section F.1 reports Transfer (naive transfer) and Transfer (cal) (calibrated transfer with N=5N\!=\!5) as representative endpoints. Tables 68 and 69 report the complete N=1,…,5N\!=\!1,\dots,5 progression alongside the Anchored same-model column for the GuardQA MLP setting. GuardQA BeaverTails Output Prediction continues to improve from 84.084.0 at N=4N\!=\!4 to 89.089.0 at N=5N\!=\!5.

F.3 Recall at 10% FPR

Same-model Standard-vs-Anchored recall parity holds for the GuardQA MLP setting (h=64h\!=\!64, 300300 anchors; Table 70). Cross-transfer recall gaps are larger than AUROC gaps, particularly on BeaverTails Output Prediction. Recall drops from 99.599.5 to 61.661.6 under naive transfer and recovers to 76.076.0 with calibration. AUROC drops from 99.899.8 to 72.372.3 and recovers to 89.089.0. The AUROC and recall results therefore show the same ordering, with larger cross-model losses at low FPR.

F.4 Alternate MLP settings

The GuardQA results above use an MLP with hidden size 6464 and 300300 anchors. This subsection tests whether same-model parity, calibrated transfer, and depth sensitivity persist under other MLP configurations.

Hidden size h=256h\!=\!256

At h=256h\!=\!256 (300300 anchors), the main cross-transfer pattern matches that at h=64h\!=\!64 (Table 71). Baseline Standard-vs-Anchored numbers differ by less than 11 AUROC point from the h=64h\!=\!64 GuardQA baseline (Table 67); we omit them here. Same-model Anchored AUROC on GT Prediction is within 0.20.2 points of h=64h\!=\!64 (marginally lower on Toxic-chat). Calibrated cross-transfer on BeaverTails Output Prediction is slightly worse (85.285.2 vs. 89.089.0 for h=64h\!=\!64); the remaining cells match within noise.

For h=256h\!=\!256, a local depth selected using target-model test data can exceed the global result on BeaverTails Output Prediction. The local probe at depth 0.850.85 reaches AUROC 89.589.5 under Transfer (cal), compared with 85.285.2 for the global probe. This is an oracle comparison. The peak at 0.850.85 is isolated. Transfer (cal) drops to 77.577.5 at depth 0.800.80 and to 74.674.6 at 0.900.90. Table 72 places this oracle result alongside validation-selected depths.

Validation-selected local-depth strategies

Table 72 compares the same validation strategies defined in Appendix C.7 against the global anchored representation for Output Prediction, for both h=64h\!=\!64 and h=256h\!=\!256 MLP probes. The Validation column uses per-model validation for same-model Anchored, per-source validation for naive Transfer, and source-pool validation for Transfer (cal). The Optimal column is selected post-hoc over the local-depth grid and uses held-out test performance.

The same-model Anchored rows change little under this choice: validation-selected local depths are close to global. For naive Transfer, source-local validation does not reliably help and is often below both fixed depth 0.80.8 and global. For Transfer (cal), source-depth validation is mixed. It improves over fixed depth 0.80.8 for the h=256h\!=\!256 BeaverTails Output slice, but hurts the h=64h\!=\!64 Output Prediction slices and slightly trails fixed depth 0.80.8 on h=256h\!=\!256 Toxic-chat Output. The Optimal column confirms that local probes can outperform global in several slices if the depth is chosen with target test labels, but the deployable Validation selector does not consistently recover those oracle depths. Thus the GuardQA analysis also supports using global anchored probes as a robust depth-free default unless transfer-depth oracle tuning is available.

Anchor count variants

Table 73 reports calibrated cross-model transfer (Transfer (cal)) as the anchor set size grows from 300 to 600, for both the MLP-64 and MLP-256 probes. Within-model performance (Standard, Anchored) is virtually unchanged across all three counts and is therefore omitted.

Cross-model transfer shows a mixed, dataset-dependent pattern. On Toxic-chat QA the effect is mildly positive. Output Prediction AUROC rises from 95.895.8 to 98.098.0 (MLP-64) and from 96.496.4 to 97.797.7 (MLP-256), while GT Prediction is flat. On BeaverTails QA, Output Prediction degrades sharply for MLP-64 (89.0→73.489.0\to 73.4) and moderately for MLP-256 (85.2→80.785.2\to 80.7). GT Prediction improves from 84.084.0 to 88.188.1 for MLP-64 and from 84.384.3 to 87.087.0 for MLP-256.

Three hundred anchors suffice for same-model parity and substantial calibrated transfer in the evaluated GuardQA configurations. Additional anchors do not yield a consistent improvement and can reduce performance, particularly for BeaverTails QA Output Prediction.

F.5 Linear probe setting

For comparison with the MLP results above, we report linear logistic-regression probes on the same GuardQA data. Linear probes leave more headroom on GT Prediction, motivating the MLP choice for the preceding GuardQA analyses.

Tables 74 and 75 show the Anchored / Transfer / Transfer (cal) summary for AUROC and recall respectively. Standard-vs-Anchored parity holds (Anchored slightly ahead on GT Prediction for both datasets). Its calibration progression follows the h=64h\!=\!64 MLP pattern: source selection helps, with the exact saturation point varying by cell. Recall cross-transfer gaps are larger than AUROC gaps, consistent with the MLP recall pattern.

F.6 Standard cross-model probe baseline

We repeat the raw-coordinate transfer test between Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B for GuardQA linear probes. Standard transfer is higher than in Trivia but still unstable, averaging 63.963.9 AUROC across datasets, probe targets, directions, and seeds; GT Prediction remains far below the anchored alternative. Under anchored global linear probes, mean cross-model AUROC rises from 63.963.9 to 84.384.3. The comparison confirms that the anchored representation restores cross-model transferability that raw coordinates lack (Tables 76 and 77).
